speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of our defence effort is to train, equip and in every way prepare our defence forces to meet the operational role which it is thought they may have to perform in order to carry out our defence policy and objectives. Consequently, like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre who spoke yesterday, I was somewhat disappointed that the minister in his speech did not place more emphasis on the training and operational phases of defence, and seemed to be more preoccupied, shall I say, with the supply, construction, and general Q and A matters concerning defence.
Canada's defence effort from the point of view of the role which our forces are to perform or may be called upon to perform has many phases or facets which connect with and run into each other. In this regard our defence effort should be compared perhaps with a cut stone with its numerous facets each of which is separate but each of which is connected with several others. Now, just as a stone has these numerous facets, so has our defence effort; and I should like to examine the operational roles or facets of our defence effort from two points of view.
The first concerns whether, considering our resources, there are too many phases with the result that they cannot all be carried out effectively. In other words, are we scattering our shot too much and as a result failing to place the emphasis in the proper places? Secondly, how effective are our forces in each of the roles they are required or may be required to carry out?
Now, the phases of our defence preparations stem, of course, from the objectives of our defence policy which have been set out for the past few years in the annual white papers. With these objectives I think practically all of us in this chamber agree. The first of these objectives is the immediate defence of Canada from direct attack, and this, of course, is the primary and most important purpose of our defence, as it is in all other countries.
The defence of Canada from direct attack must also involve the continental defence of North America. I think also we all agree that the only probable method of attack, as was stated in the white paper on defence, is by air. Now, taking that as a premise, the first phase of our defence in the role of countering an attack on Canada by air is the provision and operation of a radar screen or series of screens supplemented by a ground observer corps.
Yesterday the minister spoke of the radar screen which is in existence. He stated that
4952	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence the radar and interceptor scheme of the United States and Canada was now over 90 per cent completed and would be in complete operation by late summer or early autumn. Then he went on to say that kills in practice had been 90 per cent. He went on to say that gaps existed and that more early warning was required, that the McGill fence was going to be gone ahead with, and that the provision of all these things is extremely expensive.
However, I notice that this morning's Gazette has as its chief headline in connection with the minister's remarks one to the effect that our radar screen is 90 per cent completed and that the interception is 9 out of 10. I am afraid that this headline gives an extremely misleading idea to the House of Commons and to the Canadian people as a whole. It was pointed out yesterday by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that an American, the chairman of the joint committee on atomic energy, had pointed out that the early warning system, which was essential to the defence of both Canada and the United States, was not in existence. As a matter of fact, all that we have in the way of a radar screen, essentially, is a point system which protects us for only a short distance out. In view of the fact that enemy jet bombers would be on the targets probably within 20 minutes or a little bit more from the time they might be detected by many of the units of this radar screen, what we have gives little real protection.
There is no question that what we need is an early warning system far to the north. As was indicated in this article quoted yesterday by hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, there have been many press releases in regard to this matter, in which a great deal of information along that line has been put out, most of which-particularly that with regard to the statement made by the minister yesterday-are bound to give the public the idea that all is well from this point of view, that we are completely protected and that we have little to worry about. The average man in the street, if he reads that 9 out of 10 enemy bombers in these practice raids are being knocked out, thinks the thing must be exceptionally good and that he is quite safe. As a matter of actual fact, during the last great war in a small country like England, with a close-knit system of radar and large numbers of interceptors, the destruction of enemy bombers was approximately 1 in 10. Since that time, of course, radar has improved and jet interceptors have come into operation, and the performance is going to be considerably better. However, informed American sources
TMr. Harkness.]

whom I have seen quoted have estimated that the probable kill will be 1 in 4. The last thing I noticed in an American paper was a dispatch from Washington written by Lloyd Norman in which he says this:
Air force officials conceded that at best the air defence screen-
And this is in the United States where it is more highly developed than it is here.

could stop no more than 3 out of every 10 Russian bombers.
I think the Minister of National Defence does no service to the Canadian people by giving them a false sense of security with regard to the radar screen which exists or rather with regard to the one which does not exist. It is much better to give the actual situation in connection with the matter. I am quite sure that the Russians are not deceived in that regard. I am quite certain that they do not believe for a minute that only 1 bomber out of 10 is going to get through to the targets.
The next phase in this role of protecting Canada against air attack is the provision of interceptor planes. The minister did not say much about that matter, but we know that the number of interceptor planes in Canada is extremely small. The interceptor plane for use here is the CF-100. We know that the production of CF-lOO's so far has not been great. We know that the number of squadrons formed has been extremely small. I do not know what that number is, but I feel fairly certain that it is not more than three. That means, of course, that we have not the interceptor planes here in Canada with which to make effective use of the radar screen which does exist or the radar screen which we will have when the McGill fence and the other early warning system comes into effect. In other words, from the point of view of interceptors, at the present time we are not entirely helpless but we are very close to it, especially in large parts of this country.
The interception role in the future, according to what we have been told, is going to be carried on to quite a considerable extent by reserve force interceptor squadrons of CF-lOO's. So far these reserve squadrons have not CF-lOO's. If they had them, they would not have trained personnel who could man them and fight them effectively. One of the difficulties with regard to that matter particularly is the provision of navigators. In talking with some of the members of these reserve force interceptor squadrons which are to be equipped with CF-lOO's, I was told that they think they can train the pilots and keep them up to scratch but that it will be a more

or less impossible task for them to train the navigators and to keep them up to operational efficiency. In other words, it is the sort of thing which cannot be done by a man who spends his day working at some other occupation and does a certain amount of practice in the evenings, over week ends and so on.
It would seem fairly certain to me that if we are to have an effective interceptor force with which to make use of the radar screen, we must have in Canada considerably more regular force interceptor squadrons, whether they are CF-100 squadrons or those equipped with other planes. So far as this role is to be carried out by reserve force squadrons, they must be equipped to a greater extent than is apparently envisaged at the present time with permanent force personnel, particularly in the form of navigators.
A third phase of the defence of Canada is anti-aircraft defence to protect likely targets; that is, of course, in addition to the work of the interceptor planes. I have mentioned this matter for the last two or three years. As a matter of fact, on two or three occasions the minister has spoken of our anti-aircraft defence and I have pointed out-and I should like to do so again-that we have practically no ack-ack defence at the present time and have not had any, practically speaking, since the war. We have very few regular force personnel in active ack-ack batteries. While ack-ack defence is supposed to be carried on by reserve army anti-aircraft regiments, these reserve force ack-ack regiments have not the guns with which to do the job nor have they the personnel with which to do the job. If they had a full complement of guns they would not in most cases, in fact I think in all, even be able to look after them and man them. Apparently this situation continues to drift along from year to year. We have no "ack-ack" defence, and so far as I have been able to determine there is no improvement in the situation as time goes on. It seems to me that something definite should be done about the matter. The United States has now developed ground to air guided missiles, which are going to be the ack-ack weapons of the future, and I would hope that we might at least begin to train some people in their use and to get some of them into operation at a fairly early date.
When the minister is replying later to the various speeches that have been made, I should like him to say something about ack-ack defence and indicate what progress we have made, if any, with respect to ground to air guided missiles or even the ordinary type of rockets which can be used for that purpose. It seems to me that is one phase of the 83276-314
Supply-National Defence defence of Canadian cities and targets generally on which really nothing at all has been done so far as one can see.
The fourth phase in the protection of Canada is the provision of airborne army troops and, of course, the planes to carry them so that these troops can land at any place in the northern part of Canada where enemy landings happen to be made for the purpose of establishing an air base or something of that sort, and thus be able to wipe out an enemy effort of that kind. Considerable progress has been made in this regard. We now have three parachute battalions each with quite a large number of trained parachute troops. From what I have seen of them they are extremely good, well trained and effective battalions. However, in the event of an enemy landing anywhere in the north for the purpose of seizing a northern airfield or of establishing one, we have not got sufficient planes to transport these troops. The troops are not of a great deal of use in that particular role unless we have the planes to transport them to their targets.
In addition, they are not concentrated so that they can be operated as a brigade. I should mention of course that there are also airborne artillery forces and engineers who. I think, are also quite good, but they are scattered right across the country and it would be extremely difficult to concentrate them on a place that had been attacked. With the number of planes we have it would be a slow operation and possibly not effective. I think it was demonstrated during the last war that it is no use to move in a few plane loads of paratroopers piecemeal. By the time more plane loads arrive to reinforce them the first lot has been wiped out. It has to be done on a mass basis.
The fifth phase of the protection of Canada is the protection of coastal waters, harbour entrances and so on. I think probably this phase is more in hand than any other. We have a considerable number of naval vessels in commission that are available for this purpose, and they are probably reasonably adequate for it.
The sixth phase is the mobilization of our reserve forces for local defence and also to reinforce the regular army in the event that an enemy airborne landing is successful any place, and to guard against sabotage and so on. I am going to deal with the reserve forces later so I will not say any more at this point except to say that I do not think the reserve forces are up to this job. The reserve forces are too weak to carry out this role effectively.
Another extremely important phase of the defence of Canada is civil defence. It is
4954	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence not under the minister's department. He mentioned it briefly yesterday. I do not propose to go into the matter in detail at this time, but I see that the minister in charge of civil defence is present and I should like to say that certainly civil defence in Canada at the present time is not in any state to meet any form of attack on the country. It is perhaps the weakest link of all so far as the protection of Canada against an enemy airborne attack is concerned.
To summarize my views on the primary role of our defence forces, the direct defence of Canada, we have not got the minimum defences necessary to meet this first requirement. I think the phases of our defence effort that I have mentioned are all weak except the naval. It seems quite apparent to me that we should have put primary emphasis on these phases of our defence effort and that we have failed to do so. In other words, from both points of view that I said at the beginning I was going to discuss this matter, it is an example of failure to place emphasis at the right place and failure to succeed in the various phases or roles which I have indicated.
I have one general complaint with respect to the information given in the white paper, by the minister in his speech on these estimates and in various other speeches he has made on this matter. The public has been lulled into a false sense of security as the result of reassuring statements of every kind which do not represent the true facts of the case. I do not say that any of these statements in themselves are incorrect, but when you relate them to the general picture they give a totally false impression of what our defences are so far as the protection of Canada is concerned.
This form of misrepresentation has been going on for several years. Before the Korean conflict broke out the minister would assure the house in the defence debates that our defences were absolutely up to date-

-any possible threat.
When we were discussing the defence estimates in 1949, the year before the Korean war broke out, the minister assured us that the airborne brigade would be able to deal with any possible landing that an enemy might make in the north country. It subsequently developed-and I think a number of us knew it-that we had one battalion partially up to strength and partly trained


as parachute troops, but we did not even have the planes to transport them. Nevertheless the minister assured the house at that time that everything was fine and that we had no need to worry about any enemy landing in the north. The same sort of statements have been typical since, as was the case yesterday.
If there was any real purpose in making such statements at that time, perhaps because we were so weak, it seems to me that the time for that sort of thing has come to an end. We have improved a great deal since then. Our strength has indeed greatly increased since that period, and it would seem only reasonable to me that the house and the people of Canada should be given a true picture of the state of our defences. If they are inadequate in a particular phase or in any special way, I do not think that the minister should attempt to conceal it.
And now, the second objective of our defence policy is the implementation of the undertakings that we have made as a nation, under the United Nations and NATO, for the mutual defence of the western world. The first phase of that was our participation in the Korean war. The brigade we sent there did a magnificent job. I believe all of Canada was proud of the record that they established in Korea. Similarly, the navy did its part effectively. The air force played a part so far as the airlift was concerned, and a certain number of pilots also took part in operations with the United States air force. I feel our commitment in Korea, so far as the United Nations was concerned, was magnificently made. We were perhaps a bit slow in meeting it because of our poor state of preparation. We were able to send only one battalion at the start, but that was built up to a brigade and those who served there served well and enhanced the name of Canada in doing so.
Another phase of this implementation of our foreign commitments concerns the air division that is now in Europe and the army brigade that is in Europe. Now, that is a considerable commitment. As the minister told us yesterday the maintenance of this air division in Europe is extremely expensive, involving some $600 million. However, from an operational point of view it appears that it is an effective part of the force there, and contributes materially to the air defence of western Europe. Our army brigade is also well regarded. I shall return to these matters a little later.
Another aspect of our implementation of foreign commitments is the provision of mutual aid of various kinds, the sending of

arms to our allies and the training of NATO aircrew, things of that sort. All these things are excellent in their way, but it seems to me, from what I know of the armament of the forces in Canada, that possibly a mistake has been made by sending arms to our allies when our own forces are none too well equipped in many ways. This applies particularly to the reserve forces. It seems to me it would have been wiser, perhaps, to keep some of these arms at home until our own forces were adequately and properly equipped.
Now, to summarize, so far as the second objective of our defence is concerned, I feel our commitments have been met, and quite well met. So far as the personnel involved are concerned, I believe they are to be complimented for the manner in which they have carried out those duties. One big question arises and that is as to whether too large a proportion of the defence effort, relatively speaking, has been directed to this objective and therefore too little to the primary objective of the defence of Canada or to the third objective, the general build-up.
Yesterday two or three speakers questioned whether this division of twelve squadrons of fighter planes should be kept in Europe or whether a portion should be returned to Canada for the defence of this country, the primary role of our whole defence forces. I would question that very much, too. It seems to me that, with the speed at which these planes can be taken over to Europe, so long as the airstrips and installations to maintain the planes exist there, there is no real necessity for keeping those twelve squadrons in Europe. A good proportion of them might quite easily be kept in Canada, where they could operate in a dual role. They would be available here for immediate defence in an interceptor role of possible Canadian targets. Then, if they were needed in Europe, they could be flown over there in a matter of hours. Of course this suggestion is based on the assumption that the airfields, supply lines and so forth in Europe were kept in existence for these planes. The keeping of this full number of planes in Europe does not seem to me to be essential to carrying out our commitment to take part in the defence of western Europe.
Several speakers questioned whether the infantry brigade in Europe should not be an armoured brigade. I agree with that; I believe it should be an armoured brigade rather than an infantry brigade. It seems to me that the criticism made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre concerning the proportion of armour as compared to 83276-314i
Supply-National Defence infantry in the Canadian army was extremely sound, and that the lack of plans in that regard should be rectified.
The third objective of our defence policy is to build up strength for total war. All of the phases of our defence effort that I have mentioned previously, of course, enter into this and are part of it. But there are some which are perhaps more directly and entirely related to the build-up, as you might call it. One of these is the build-up of staffs and service units of all kinds. I believe that one of the mistakes that have been made is the multiplication of staffs. There has been far too great a multiplication of staffs and too much manpower has been devoted to staffs of all sorts. As I have mentioned here several times before in previous years, you have only to look at the telephone directory to see the various staffs at national headquarters, and you gain some idea of the tremendous number of people who are carrying on activities there, in some cases activities not very much greater than was the case before the second great war, but with a staff ten or twenty times as great as existed at that time. This is one of the places where I think the emphasis has been misdirected. At the same time the civilian staffs have greatly increased this year. They have been increasing year after year, and it seems to me far too much manpower is used in pushing paper back and forth. The paper war should be cut down to a minimum, but the multiplication of these staffs really increases it. The amount of office supplies purchased is an indication of the enormous amount of paper work, and I am quite sure much of it is not really necessary, in fact it cannot help but clog the defence effort.
Another phase is construction activities, the provision of barracks, married quarters, storage space, the building of airfields and things of that sort. Once again I believe there has been too much emphasis on this subject. It is a good thing to have good barracks, to have ample storage space, to have fine married quarters and so on, and I am saying nothing against it. It seems to me, however, that the emphasis has been misplaced and there are other things that are more important, such as the provision of tanks for our armoured corps, the provision of the most modern arms of all sorts, which have not been provided, although there has been this large expenditure on construction activities. These construction activities, the minister indicated, are tapering off. It seems to me that is one place where a considerable saving in defence expenditures should be possible. The amount of building for married quarters still to be completed under the plan
4956	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence is not so great. The major portion of that program is over. The major portion of the barracks building program is over, and the same applies to the building of airfields. So that I would hope much less would be expended under the construction program in the .years ahead, and the money so saved directed into other channels, if the general expenditures are not, indeed, reduced as a result.
Another phase is the build-up of mobilization stores. A great deal of the criticism of the Department of National Defence last year was in regard to the enormous amount of soft goods, as they are called, which were purchased. I think without question there are many examples of waste and extravagance in the amount of soft goods purchased, including such things as raincoats, boots and the like.
The minister said in his speech-or it might have been mentioned in the white paper, I am not sure which-that the build-up of mobilization stores of soft goods is almost complete. Well, I would think it would be complete, in view of the very large quantities purchased in the last two years or so. He has said that weapons, ammunition and equipment for mobilization have been built up. I notice that the amounts for these for the army, the navy and the air force are down this year in many cases from what they were last year. I would hope this does not mean that some of the essential armaments of modern warfare, which our forces should have if they are going to be able to discharge their function effectively, are not being purchased or secured. I would refer particularly to some of the later types of guns, both ack-ack and anti-tank, to tanks and things of that nature.
Perhaps the most important phase of the general build-up of strength is in the reserve forces. They continue to be, as they have been in the past, the framework upon which the mobilization of Canadian manpower, particularly in the Canadian army, must depend. It seems to me that the army reserve force, in particular, has been one of the outstanding failures of the defence department in recent years. We have heard complaints from reserve force officers and personnel, and there has been considerable discussion in the house in the last several years as to the poor state of the reserve forces. The government was sufficiently impressed with what was said to appoint a committee, known as the Kennedy committee, which spent a good part of last year investigating the situation in respect of the reserve army. That committee presented a report, and I am disappointed to find that the minister has not made that report public, so that we can find out what,


in the opinion of experts, are the difficulties in connection with the reserve forces, and the recommendations as to how those forces could be improved.
In his speech the minister said he would deal with the reserves at a later time, when we reach the item in the estimates. I hope when he does so he will place on record the results of the Kennedy report, and the recommendations made.
The figures given as to the numbers in the reserve force, so far as the army is concerned, are practically the same this year as they were last. The figures shown at page 84 of the report indicate that there were approximately fifty fewer registered in the reserve army in 1952-53 than there were in 1951-52. The figures also indicate that there has been a small increase in the navy, and a larger one in the air force where there has been an increase from 4,800 to 5,800.
I cannot speak with authority so far as the navy and air force reserves are concerned, but I would say that, with respect to the army reserves, these figures do not mean very much, and one cannot draw any conclusions from them. I do know that the units with which I am familiar-and I believe the same applies right across Canada-are fairly well up to strength in the matter of officers. As the minister indicated, there has been a big officer training scheme and the reserve units have no difficulties so far as the supply of officers is concerned. But they are woefully weak from the standpoint of the rank and file enlistments. As a result of that, they are not able to carry on their training effectively and could not undertake any operational role. In addition to that, they have suffered from lack of equipment.
In many cases the equipment they have had has been old and out of date. This has been discouraging to those who have been recruited, and it has prevented their remaining with the units. I have here a letter from a former non-commissioned officer of the Calgary Highlanders in which he makes a few comments concerning the reserve army which in my view indicate clearly the views of a large number in the rank and file of reserve units. It sets out the reasons why in many cases they do not continue. I should like to read a few excerpts from it.
He says:
The argument that there are not enough men serving with keenness is just a condemnation of the policies that have governed the reserve till now. Build up morale and the reserve will build up.
We have been trying to impress that upon the minister and the government ever since the close of the last war. Unless the young men of this country feel that there is a real

need for their services in reserve units, and that they are doing a real job in those units, we will not get recruits. There has never been any real effort to impress that fact upon the consciousness of the young men of this country. The letter goes on to say this:
Men join the reserve to work; take them at their word; I never heard a man complain about too much work at any time during my service. Idle periods spoil morale.
One of the reasons there are idle periods in the reserve forces is that there are not enough men to carry on training in many of the phases which should foe carried on. As a result of this, much time is wasted. The letter continues:
They have obsolescent equipment; nothing is more discouraging than to instruct or be instructed on equipment that we all know perfectly well we shall never use in earnest; just wasted time.
This comes back to the amount of equipment we have sent overseas to our allies. While I do not complain about that policy, as I said previously I think we should equip our own forces, including our reserve forces, with up to date equipment before we send equipment overseas. Certainly we should not have the situation we have had, where equipment was sent overseas and units in Canada have been left without it. This has been true particularly in the case of a large number of anti-tank regiments and batteries throughout the country.
Then the letter continues:
Pay should be free of Income tax. Often his reserve pay puts him into a higher tax bracket so he loses quite a proportion of his pay.
That is a matter we have discussed repeatedly. It was mentioned last night by the hon. member for Oxford, when he was referring to the naval reserve force. I do not think there is any question about it; it is one of the causes of discontent which has an effect out of all proportion to the amount of money involved. A large number of people serving in the reserve feel extremely keenly on this point. They do not think they should be taxed on the amount of money they get for the reserve force training. In many instances, the real advantage to them, the amount of take-home pay they get after taking part in various social activities in connection with their service, is very small. As I say, the amount of revenue which the government receives from it is small, and is out of all proportion to the discontent it causes. I would once more urge the government to give consideration to the matter of making reserve force pay exempt for income tax purposes up to a reasonable amount at any rate. The man in the reserve force who is on call-outs, or otherwise puts in a good portion of the year, say a quarter or a half
Supply-National Defence of the year, as some have done, makes quite an income. Then the argument in connection with collecting income tax on it is a different matter altogether; but the ordinary man in the reserve who draws 15 or 25 days' pay a year should be exempt.
The minister's general appreciation of the probabilities in the future-that there is no real change in the fundamental Soviet objectives; that the fear of mass destruction in the A and H-bombs is a powerful deterrent to general war; that the massive destructiveness of those bombs may be the opposite to a deterrent in small wars; and that the existence of those bombs does not remove the need for conventional arms-is an appreciation with which I think most of us will agree. However, once that is accepted, it seems to me that the general strategical thinking perhaps has not been geared to that. It is quite evident that we must be prepared to meet an A and H-bomb attack, and to meet that the chief features are the defence of Canada itself that I mentioned earlier. To meet our commitments under the United Nations and NATO we must be prepared apparently to participate in small wars with conventional weapons.
It seems to me that the general thinking in preparations which have been made by the Department of National Defence has given too little attention to the first of those roles which our defence forces have to take on, and too much to the second, namely, participation with conventional weapons in small wars. As a matter of fact, it would seem from the way in which expansion has taken place in the army that the thinking is almost pre-world-war II rather than up to date.
The minister stated that we now have fifteen battalions of infantry. We have of course still only two regiments of armour.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to make a few remarks on these estimates. They are the most difficult estimates that come before the house for an ordinary member to deal with, in my opinion. In my opening remarks I must say that I wholeheartedly support the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
We in this group support all necessary expenditures to provide adequate defence for this country, but we are very much opposed to unnecessary expenditure in any respect whatever. We were told some three years ago that we would have a defence program for a three-year period, with an expenditure of about $5 billion. I am quite sure that at that time we got the impression that once we had the three-year program pretty well completed and the $5 billion expended we would then be over the hump and the people of Canada could look forward to some reduction in taxation as a result of the lessening of defence expenditures. The minister informed us yesterday that we have to be prepared for what I think he termed "a long haul" at about the present rate of expenditure. We in this group are not convinced that the present rate of expenditure is required to provide adequate defence for this country. We take that view for several reasons. First, I think we are on sound ground, because history proves that no general staff ever asked for a reduction of any defence estimates. It is only natural that those who are engaged in those activities are anxious to maintain their prestige, their positions and things of that sort. It is further proven by the remarks of the hon. member for Esqui-malt-Saanich, as reported at page 2810 of Hansard of 1951, when he said:
I have never known an admiral, a general or an air marshal who did not begin by asking for more than his share of anything.

maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS FROM NEW WESTMINSTER BRANCH, CANADIAN LEGION
speechtext: Send them to the cleaners.

The staff at defence headquarters immediately sprang to the defence of the minister's trousers by issuing the following order, and I am now going to quote this order which was taken from the bulletin board in the national defence headquarters: All Officers, D Pers Carrying of Parcels
(1)	The Minister of National Defence has ruled that there will he no more carrying of large baskets or boxes of coffee or food in the buildings occupied by national defence headquarters.
(2)	There is no objection to the transportation of a single cup of coffee from one office to another when the need arises.
This was signed by L. L. Mathers (F. LeP. T. Clifford), Colonel, director of army personnel.
I understand that the result of the minister's order has been that instead of 10 cups of coffee being taken at the same time from the basement up to, say, the third storey offices, they have to carry one cup of coffee at a time. Now, just imagine an orderly going upstairs with one cup of coffee at a time.
My point is this, though this may seem only a minor incident, that if this is the general
Supply-National Defence staff's idea of the utilization of manpower when they issue an order, then it is a rather sorry one, because it means 10 times more labour is required than was required formerly for "Operation Coffee". Under such circumstances we have every reason and good grounds to suspect that we are not getting value for the defence dollar.

I would like to refer to another small incident. In answer to a question I asked in the house I was informed by the minister's parliamentary assistant that 36 pairs of skates were purchased for the College Militaire Royal de Saint Jean at a total cost of $1,224 or $34 per pair for the cadets in this military college. First of all I want to know why this government is buying skates for cadets who are reasonably paid by the Canadian taxpayer. Secondly, I want to know why they bought luxury skates. There are not very many people in Canada who can purchase skates at $34 per pair,
I think this is another illustration of a completely unnecessary expenditure in the Department of National Defence. Now, I want to mention one more incident, though I admit quite frankly it is a small incident. Nevertheless, it does indicate a state of mind, and disregard of economy.
Not long ago three generals came to the parliamentary restaurant to fulfil, I presume, a social engagement. I do not know whether it was for tea or dinner, but in any event the three generals came from defence headquarters in three beautiful and expensive cars driven by three chauffeurs. They all arrived in their grandeur complete with the three chauffeurs who had to wait outside the parliament building for about two hours.
My point is this. Ministers of the crown in a democracy are senior to the members of the general staff in regard to order of precedence and, in fact, members of parliament are senior in order of precedence to the chief of the general staff, and rightly so. But if our cabinet ministers, and I give them credit for this, can travel around in cars which cost a very modest amount without chauffeurs, surely we do not require such expensive cars for senior officers of the Department of National Defence often used unnecessarily.
I have mentioned three small incidents all of which indicate a certain trend and they

Supply-National Defence are only what we can see on the surface. We can only see the pimples of expense but therefore judge that the carbuncles are somewhat large in size.
I am not going to speak at length but I would now like to turn to something I think should be drawn to the attention of the minister. I am referring to the case of Kurt Meyer, whose kind treatment raised some objection in Canada recently. That matter is now closed. I think we had our legs pulled to some extent by the government in this case. This German general was found guilty of having incited and counselled troops under his command to deny quarter to allied troops and to be responsible for the killing of Canadian prisoners of war. The death sentence imposed by the court was commuted by General Vokes to life imprisonment. A reviewing board without any Canadian members has since granted remission of sentence which will mean that this nazi German general will be released in a few months.
My point is this. If this nazi general can receive that sort of compassion and his sentence can be reviewed by a board with the consent of the Canadian government, surely the same compassion should be shown to servicemen found guilty by courts-martial of far lesser offences during wartime and for which their punishment continues.
That is my argument, Mr. Chairman, and on that account I urge in all fairness and justice that there should be a review of these cases. Many servicemen are still undergoing sentence imposed during the war and they should be shown the same compassion as that shown to Kurt Meyer. Officers who were cashiered should have their sentences reviewed with a view to imposing a much lighter sentence than dismissal from the service.
Officers who were cashiered are now and will be forever barred from holding public office, which for any person is a terrible penalty. It must be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that these officers were volunteers who came direct from military colleges, from business life, or from the ranks, and they had little or no experience of the heavy responsibilities entailed.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that there are many men who are suffering today from sentences imposed during the war and whose cases now in all fairness should be reviewed. When our government can approve a remission of sentence to a general responsible for counselling the killing of Canadian soldiers, surely the government should in justice and in fairness review the cases of the men who are suffering at the present time for lesser crimes committed during the war. I urge a reexamination of these cases and consideration
[Mr. Herridge.l

on behalf of these unfortunate men who are still suffering and will continue to suffer unless something is done.
In concluding I want to make just a few remarks concerning enlistment and examinations for enlistment because I have knowledge of some unfortunate circumstances and cases. I have personal knowledge of an unfortunate case which would not have occurred, in my opinion, if the Department of National Defence had been more careful in examining the young man to whom I have reference, who was in Essondale for a number of years. I may say that Essondale is our mental asylum in British Columbia. He was enlisted in the army, later committed a crime in the United States, was sentenced to life imprisonment and is serving that sentence in the United States at this time. So far nothing has been done to restore that young man to Canadian custody. I mention this case because I think it is a most unfortunate one. I am not suggesting that there are many, but when cases like this one can occur I suggest that there must be something wrong in connection with the examination of men seeking to enlist in the armed forces.
In this connection I want to read briefly from an editorial in the Globe and Mail of Friday, April 2, 1954. It is headed "The Real Question" and reads as follows:
Parliament finally got around to the case of Private Walter Cierpisz on Wednesday, when a socialist member . . .
That is myself, I presume.
. . . asked whether the defence department took any precautions against the enlistment of mental defectives in the armed forces. (Cierpisz, now serving ten years for manslaughter, was described at his trial as having a mental age of ten.)
The answer given by Associate Defence Minister Campney suggests that, in his view, Canada's parliament and people are mentally defective. Certainly they would need to be, to swallow the miserable excuses he put forward. Claiming that each of the services gave careful mental and physical tests to prospective recruits, Mr. Campney continued:
"Those who pass them must be far beyond the mental age of ten. The tests are carefully worked out, and have resulted extremely well in most cases. Of course, there will always be borderline cases wherever the line is drawn. Some borderline cases turn out very well and some not so well. This is one of the unfortunate ones."
If Cierpisz, with a mental age of ten, was a borderline case, where is the border, and what is the line? Are we to assume that recruits with a mental age of 11 or 12 are considered safely past, or indeed "far beyond" it? In any event, was Cierpisz given the official tests, and by whom? Did he actually pass them, and by whose judgment? . . .
Parliament must look further up in the defence department. Who makes and supervises appointments to examining bodies of this nature? How is the screening of recruits checked, if it is checked at all? Not until these questions have been

answered can we determine who, and at what level, is responsible for the enlistment of men who should never have been enlisted.
I quote from that editorial, Mr. Chairman, because I agree with the suggestions contained in it. When the minister speaks in reply to the criticisms made from this side of the chamber, I should like him to inform the committee of the procedure in connection with examining a man on his application for enlistment into the defence forces.
Once again I want to say that we on this side of the chamber-with the exception possibly of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and one or two others-are at a great disadvantage in criticizing these estimates with knowledge and with certainty. We know this expenditure is a terrific burden on the Canadian people but we cannot discharge our duty adequately by a general discussion during the estimates, while the house is sitting. I certainly think we require a continuing defence committee composed of members of all parties, taken into the confidence of the Department of National Defence and having an opportunity to make certain that every dollar that is spent is necessary for the adequate defence of this country.

maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS FROM NEW WESTMINSTER BRANCH, CANADIAN LEGION

It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to occupy the time of the committee for long. However, there are certain matters on which I believe I should comment at this time. Yesterday the Minister of National Defence laid down, in clear and precise terms, Canada's defence policy. He dealt with internal defence and he dealt with our defence from the standpoint of our activities in association with our allies. What was said by him, supplemented by the white paper, gave us a reasonably clear over-all picture of policy. However, I think even the minister would agree that much detail was missing.
I want to concur wholeheartedly in the observation made by the hon. member for Kootenay West and by practically every other member who has spoken with respect to the necessity for the establishment of what I would call a standing committee on defence rather than a defence expenditure committee. Because of what has taken place in the past I fully realize that the name "defence expenditure committee" might cause the minister to bristle just a wee bit, but not if it were a defence committee, an all-party committee, charged with the responsibility of dealing with the estimates and of even dealing with expenditures. Where it seems, in the opinion of the committee members, that such examination is necessary-that is as to expenditure with respect to some specific matter-they should be authorized to pursue the study of that matter.
Supply-National Defence
Certainly practically all members of the House of Commons find themselves in a most unfortunate position when it comes to consideration of these estimates. Actually, if we were to do justice to these estimates we would keep the minister and the committee here for days, weeks and even months. After all, let us just consider for one moment what part of the total budget is devoted to national defence. If we look at it in no other way, from the taxpayers' point of view we would be completely justified in devoting, as I say, even weeks or months to the consideration of that department alone. I certainly suggest, for several reasons, that the minister urge the government to give favourable consideration to the setting up of that committee which would be a standing committee and which could sit almost continuously while parliament is in session.
After all, we have other committees. We realize that even though the Secretary of State for External Affairs from time to time makes comprehensive statements on the floor of the House of Commons, certain of his estimates are referred to the external affairs committee and witnesses are called before that committee. Those who are members of that committee will secure much information from the witnesses and we who may not be members of the committee will certainly have the benefit of the printed evidence. But possibly of even more importance than that, the Canadian taxpayers will have an opportunity of securing copies of that evidence.
Important as defence may be, I cannot lose sight of the fact that the Canadian taxpayers are bearing a colossal burden for defence. Times are reasonably buoyant now. Even though that is so, yesterday the minister stated that the burdens laid upon this country by national defence are heavy, even in relation to our immense resources. He might also have added "even in relation to the general economic picture in the country today". We have no assurance that the general economic picture will continue to be as favourable as it is at the present time. Yet the demands for adequate defence may make it completely impossible to cut back even though there may at some time be a general deterioration in the economic picture. My personal conviction is that as long as international tension continues, as long as the avowed purpose of the communists is what it is today, as long as their actions continue to give the lie to their words, we will not only have to maintain our defences at the present level but will most undoubtedly have to expand them as time goes on. I think it
4962	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence would give a good deal of comfort and satisfaction to the Canadian taxpayers, and certainly to a good many members of the house, if such a committee were set up.
May I suggest to the minister that I think the onus is upon him to give us reasons, if there are such, for not setting up a committee on national defence. Certainly he is aware of the widespread demand from this part of the house. With reference to the lack of information, may I say that it applies not only to members of the house but also to the Canadian people, and undoubtedly much of the criticism that falls upon the minister's shoulders from time to time results directly from the fact that the Canadian people are not as fully informed as they should be.
Let me give an illustration or two in order to be quite specific. There were two fires recently at Canadian air stations, and investigations were made with respect to them. May I clarify a certain matter right at this point. Members who were in the house prior to the last election will recall that from time to time I offered severe criticism of certain things that were happening with respect to defence construction at Penhold in my constituency. I am still absolutely convinced that I was completely justified in doing so. I do not have to go beyond the words of the present Minister of Public Works to believe that much good resulted from what I said on the floor of the house.
But this is what I want to point out. Last summer certain friends of the government went out of their way to create the impression that what I did on the floor of the house with respect to Penhold was to criticize the Royal Canadian Air Force as such. I say that accusation is wholly false. I have had the greatest admiration for the Royal Canadian Air Force both during the war and in the period subsequent to the war. As far as I am able to determine, the Penhold air station is operating in a most satisfactory manner. From what I have learned I am confident that the officers are carrying out their work in a most satisfactory way and are deserving of commendation. Let it not be said again, in the light of what I am going to say now, that I am offering criticism of the Royal Canadian Air Force. I realize fully that they operate under certain rules and regulations which at times may leave them in a position where it may appear that they may be responsible for things for which they are not responsible.
Having said that, may I refer to the rather disastrous fire that occurred at Penhold on April 10 which resulted in the destruction of a hangar in which there were a number of


service aircraft. All I have to go on of course are the press reports. It was indicated that it was a million dollar fire. That may be quite wrong, but that is the information I have and that is the information the public has. On May 3 I asked on the floor of the house if the investigation into the fire had been completed and, if so, whether the report would be tabled in the house. I realized when I asked the question that there was slight possibility of the report being tabled because apparently it is not government policy to do so.
I should like to ask the minister this question. Why should it be the policy not to table the report of such an investigation as that into the fire at Penhold? That is a question that a great many people would like to have answered. Why? When police investigations take place into certain things the information is made available to the public. Because of the fact that the people do not know any more than they saw at the time or read in the newspapers, two stories are current. One is that if the wind had been blowing from the opposite direction there might have been very little of Penhold air station left. I did not happen to be home at the time, but persons who were present have indicated to me that that might well have been the disastrous result. It was also indicated that at the end of the fire and before the hangar was destroyed the people fighting it were completely without water. If that is true it simply means that maybe we have not made adequate provision for fire protection.
I think these are things that the minister should clarify. I am not making these remarks in any critical sense. We have a wonderful station at Penhold. The Canadian taxpayers have quite a few millions of dollars invested in other air stations and installations across Canada. I believe it is the practice of the government to carry its own insurance with the result that a million dollar loss in a fire simply means a million dollars lost to the Canadian taxpayers. I trust the minister will be able to assure the house that adequate fire fighting facilities are established at these stations.
Even more important than that, I have before me a short editorial that appeared in the Albertan, a Calgary daily paper, the issue of April 13, and in it a few questions are asked. I suppose they probably would not have been asked if the answers were known. Certainly I cannot answer them on the basis of the knowledge I have now. The editorial reads as follows:
We would like to know what system of fire watches is maintained at R.C.A.F. stations.

Then they refer to Penhold and ask this question:
... is there one man on duty at all times at each hangar, or does one man have to keep watch on several hangars? We gather from the news reports that the latter condition exists. Loss was at least a million dollars at Penhold when fire destroyed one of the hangars and its contents over the week end. It is reasonable to believe that if one man had been assigned to that building alone, patrolling all corners of it, the fire would have been detected in time to control it.
Any privately owned building worth a million dollars has a watchman on duty every hour of the day, every day of the year. Isn't public property worth just as much protection? Should the authorities take unnecessary chances just because the taxpayers can be counted on to make up the loss. There are reported to be about 3,000 men at the Penhold station. Surely it wouldn't be a hardship on the personnel to have someone in each hangar at all times.
What the policy is across Canada I do not know, but I think we should know. Of course, if it had been generally known at that time I doubt if these questions would have been asked by the Albertan in this editorial. I trust that the minister will bear that in mind. I am not concerned specifically with Penhold. That sort of fire could occur anywhere. As I say, I am concerned about the water supply. I know that we paid plenty for a water supply there. I am also concerned about the consequences of what the people who were there say would have happened if the wind had been in the opposite direction. I say to the minister that personally I cannot understand why reports of investigations of this kind should not be made public. I think it would ease the public mind. It is not just a question of trying to attach blame to somebody. I am not trying to attach blame to anyone. Whatever is done is done because of policy. The fire watch at Penhold, whatever it was, I asume must have been the same as that in existence at other air stations. It may be good, but we do not know what the general policy is.
There is another matter that I feel the minister should bear in mind. I can judge the importance of this only by the number of letters which have come to me from parents. The minister will understand that I am not in a position to table the letters, so I shall not quote them. They are from the parents of persons in the air force, and certainly I am not going to even run the risk of jeopardizing their welfare by naming them. Recently, while the minister was away, I asked the Associate Minister of National Defence this question. These are not exact words, but it was something like this: Does the government intend grounding all jet aircraft in Canada pending an investigation into the crashes that have taken place within recent times? The associate minister indicated that
Supply-National Defence there were several types of jet aircraft, and therefore it would be rather senseless to ground them all. Perhaps I should have been more explicit in my question and mentioned the specific type of aircraft or asked in my question that the particular type of jet aircraft that is causing the difficulties be grounded.
I am advised with respect to these crashes that we do not know about all of them. I should like to know the total number of crashes there have been in Canada of jet aircraft, say within the last six months. This seems to have been a particularly bad period.
I should like the information concerning accidents to jet aircraft, not only in which airmen have been killed, but accidents on the ground. I am told by the parents of young men in the air force, who were told by their sons, that the information is kept completely away from these young men. What they learn they hear over the air or pick up in the newspaper, even though it may be an accident in connection with their own station. They say it is extremely detrimental to morale. I can easily understand how it could be detrimental to morale.
I feel the minister should give this house a clearly-defined picture of the actual amount of training an airman gets before he solos in a jet aircraft. I am not suggesting for a moment that the information I have is correct, but once again it comes from parents whose sons have indicated to them that it is their conviction they are compelled to solo much too soon so far as these jet aircraft are concerned. They get a certain amount of training with Harvards. I am told that after they get that training with Harvards they are given six hours' dual instruction on a jet, and then they are on their own. That is the statement that comes from the parent of one of the boys who is flying a jet. I do not know enough about jet aircraft to know whether or not six hours' dual flying, even though they have had the training in the conventional type of aircraft, is sufficient. Certainly, something is wrong somewhere when one stops to contemplate the accidents that have occurred in connection with jet aircraft in Canada. I trust the minister will try to satisfy us with respect to this matter. These and many other things are based on the lack of specific information before me and before the Canadian public.
I think that probably even before now either the minister or the Associate Minister of National Defence should have been right up on his feet to make a statement with respect to these jet aircraft crashes. I think it would certainly result in much higher morale among the service personnel, more

Supply-National Defence particularly among the younger lads. I know one parent wrote to me and said: For goodness' sake, until they find out what is wrong with these jets, put the older, more experienced pilots into them and not my young lad of 21 with the training he has had. He said he just sits in fear awaiting that telegram to come, and he would be much happier if he knew that for this period, while they are having some trouble, they would keep these young lads out of jet aircraft.
Actually, I did not intend to speak so long. I did not try to deal with defence policy. My colleague the hon. member for Wetaskiwin dealt with that. He made it abundantly clear to the house that we believe Canada should be as adequately defended as possible. As he said, it is not how much we spend, but how we spend it that counts. The government has had no trouble from us when it has come to securing support for defence appropriations. We do, however, feel that the greatest value should be procured for every dollar spent. We do feel, as other members have stated, that so far as we are concerned there is no justification for failure to set up that defence committee. After all, let me repeat, more than $2 billion has been appropriated for defence this year; that is a substantial part of our 1954-55 national budget. If we can take time to have other committees studying other aspects of government operations, then how much more important is it for us to have a defence committee for the purpose of examining into defence.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we come to the annual debate on the estimates for the Department of National Defence we cover a lot of ground from the personnel, strategic and tactical standpoints, so that one could

speak for a very long time on this aspect of our security. It is not my purpose to go into higher strategy-although I could-or the tactics we have developed to defend this country. That has been gone into by other speakers, and I shall not repeat it today.
However, listening to the minister yesterday one could not help being struck by the position in which this continent finds itself, when he described the terrific power of the A-bomb, and now the hydrogen bomb-and I suppose in a short time it will be the C-bomb. This power of destruction is so great, we have been told, as to stagger the imagination of the ordinary human being. But let me say immediately that all down through the history of war, its basic principles never change, although the means of waging it have changed.
This massive power of destruction which we have is only a continuation of the powers of destruction we have had in modern times. It is something to consider very seriously, and something to drive home in the minds of our people so that they will be fully informed of the dangers which lie at their door, if a third world war were to take place.
We all know that Russian aircraft can reach this continent. We also know that, with all our defences, some of the aircraft will get through. That is a serious situation for people living in the large cities on this continent. It is a situation which I know concerns the heads of our services, and one with which they are grappling all the time. It is a condition with which this and other countries are grappling conscientiously at all times. Nevertheless some of those aircraft will get through. And with that situation, I think we have to face up to the fact that our civilian population should be warned sufficiently so that they may take adequate steps to minimize this danger which confronts us today.
To bear out my point, may I quote from page 4905 of Hansard, what was said by the minister. He said:
It is very risky for people charged with defence to make a prophecy. All we can do is to give opinions and not give assurances, but this system of defence against air attack has reached the stage today where if I were in charge of the Russian air force and were aiming to reach important targets in the United States-
And I am sorry he did not mention Canada. -I would not go across the lines of these radar defences. I would go some other way-
And he ends with the words, "and there are other ways". That, to me, if it means anything, means that with all our defences-and they are good; I have seen them myself and I think they are manned by capable aircrew-we are vulnerable. Because if there
Supply-National Defence are other ways, we must be vulnerable. I do not want the minister to give any hint as to what the other ways are. I would not expect that. I do not want him to say it, and I do not want to know it. But that significant statement made yesterday by the minister is something which should be brought home to every man, woman and child in this country- that we are vulnerable.
I come from a province which is vital to the defence of Canada. This afternoon, if I may, I want to confine myself to a problem which, as I see it, confronts us on the eastern seaboard. It was only last Sunday that we, together with the armed forces, celebrated the anniversary of the battle of the Atlantic. We know that we won that battle only by a very short hair. Sir Winston Churchill, in his memoirs, has said that it was touch and go. And there is danger in the Atlantic today, just as much as there was during the second world war. I refer to the submarine menace.
Now, I know we have improved our methods of submarine detection. I also know that the menace is there today, just as much as it ever was. With the modern submarine, and with methods of detection, the menace still exists. Let me say right here and now that it is only two or three years ago that Russian submarines were in the bay of Fundy and around the coast of Newfoundland. I know the number that were there, but I will not mention it. However, I do know they were there-and they were there for no good, so far as we are concerned.
The latest development is that of Russian trawlers fishing on the Grand Banks. I wish to refer to this visit to the Grand Banks which took place a short time ago, because to me it seems that it shows a certain amount of slackness in our military forces in the province from which I come. I shall try to bring out this point.
In this connection I quote from the Evening Telegram of St. John's, which says:
U.S. Intelligence, the R.C.A.F. and "certain authorities" are expressing keen interest in the goings-on of two Russian trawlers on the Grand Banks.
U.S.A.F. and R.C.A.F. planes have flown over the trawlers-Odessa and Sevastapol, which are partially "manned" by women-and the R.C.A.F. took some aerial photographs of them.
Meanwhile captain of the Spanish trawler "Euskal-Erria" has taken sea-level pictures of the Russian ships and taken these photos to "certain authorities in Newfoundland" and to U.S. Intelligence at Pepperrell base.
It goes on:
F/O Lloyd admitted that most of the information available to the R.C.A.F. in Newfoundland and Halifax, maybe Ottawa, now too, was gleaned from Evening Telegram investigations and reportorial accounts.
4966	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence
In other words the first word our intelligence officers in Newfoundland had was this article in the Evening Telegram. It states further:
Commodore Gabriel Aguirre of the Spanish fishing fleet told the Telegram his subordinates reported to "certain authorities" in St. John's, giving those "certain authorities" photographs and getting in return (for better pictures) a better camera than that which they were using, so as to get more pictures of the Russians at the Banks.
And it ends in this way:
Russian trawlers aren't on the Grand Banks to fish. They're there for information relevant to our coastal waters, defences and the like, Commodore Aguirre said in an exclusive Evening Telegram interview.
W/C Pleasance, head over the R.C.A.F. here, said last night he didn't know too much about the Russian ships ". . . and I'd like to know more."
If that means anything to me it means that the Russian ships were fishing on the Grand Banks for some time before our authorities knew anything at all about it. The first intimation they had that the Russians were there was when this Spanish commodore came into St. John's, Newfoundland, for supplies and notified the authorities. That brings me to a recommendation which I intend to make now. In this fishing fleet on the Grand Banks, which is composed of Portuguese, Spanish, French and other trawlers those countries have vessels on patrol for their protection. I think the time has now come, indeed if it is not overdue, when we must have a warship of some form on the Grand Banks watching what is going on there. It would be useful to our own fishing fleet; certainly they need some protection in case of emergency, and to keep an eye on the Russian trawlers coming out fishing there. We know, regardless of how much we should like to think otherwise, that they are not there for our good. First of all we had a submarine, and now we have Russian trawlers. I am convinced they are not there to fish. They have plenty of places to fish without coming to the Grand Banks.
This brings me to another point. Newfoundland is, as all hon. members know, an island. It is also known, as I mentioned a moment ago, that the submarine menace is a serious one. If we do get into a third world war, which I hope we will not, there will be hell on the Atlantic. We had hell on the Atlantic before, and we in Newfoundland know it because hundreds of seamen who were rescued from the icy waters of the Atlantic were brought to our shores, and it was almost a daily occurrence. Furthermore, iron ore ships were torpedoed in Conception bay, not far from my home, with a great loss of life. They were torpedoed right in front of people living there. Only the other day it was reported in the papers


that a submarine in the English channel on manoeuvres had disappeared. An alarm was sent out that it had not reported for some time. They thought it was in difficulty, but later it surfaced. It had eluded all the craft that were searching for it. They were searching for the submarine with the latest modern submarine detection equipment. If that could happen on manoeuvres in the English channel it gives us some idea of the danger that the submarine menace is to our security today. I could give other examples of that but I do not want to do it here in the committee because I do not want to give any comfort to the enemy, no matter who he may be. It is my firm conviction that the submarine menace is a serious one. The position in which my province finds itself is this, if we should ever get into a third world war, we are dependent almost wholly on the sea for our supplies. If this menace is as bad or as serious as I think it is we shall have to supply our troops in Germany largely by air. We have not the airports in Newfoundland or Labrador to take care of the traffic that would have to be accommodated.
I was told about two or three years ago by those who knew that another airport should be built in Newfoundland. It was not built. I was at Gander at the time and I was told on very good authority that if we ever got into a war Gander could not carry the traffic and neither could Goose, and another airport was needed to carry the prospective traffic. It is a vital necessity. I bring it to the attention of the authorities. I do not want Canada to do it if she is not able to do it. She might make some arrangements with the United States. The United States already have two airports there, one at Harmon field on the west coast and the other at Marquise near the naval base at Argentia. We have Gander and Torbay, and Goose in Labrador. So great will be this traffic going by air that we will not have the facilities to carry it. To me it is going to be a serious thing. I think the time to prepare for it is now; therefore I bring it to the attention of the minister. I am not criticizing him or his department; I am just bringing it to his attention because if this happens, as I see it, then you will have to supply the people of Newfoundland by air. That is the only way you will be able to get the supplies in.
I could go farther and recommend where the airport should be, but I shall leave that to the people who are supposed to pick out the places and when they do probably I shall have something more to say on the matter. I do want to bring that to the serious consideration of the minister. It is serious to our people in Newfoundland and

it is serious to Canada. Newfoundland is the Gibraltar of the Atlantic. It played a vital part in the convoy system during the last war, and it will play a greater part if we ever get into a third world war. I want to bring that with all the emphasis I can to the attention of hon. members.
To bear out what I am trying to say and to try to emphasize it I am going to quote from the remarks of the minister which he made yesterday in a very frank way. He said, as reported at page 4905 of Hansard:
When we were up in the Arctic four weeks ago I was astonished to find that to keep a weather station employing nine men going took 340 tons of supplies a year, and that involved 30 round trips of a North Star aircraft from Resolute Bay to wherever the station was. It also involved getting the supplies to Resolute by aircraft or ship. When we have to use 30 round trips of a heavy transport over these immense distances to supply a station employing nine men you can see how tremendous will be the task of increasing our defences in the far north. However, I am sure that more will have to be done and that it will be done.
If it takes 340 tons of supplies to supply nine men, how many tons of supplies will be needed to supply the people of Newfoundland, to keep life in them, because you will not get supplies in by sea. The only way will be by air. I quote that statement to emphasize the point which I am trying to make here this afternoon.
Others have mentioned the tremendous cost of this defence, roughly $2 billion a year. We are all very much concerned with these tremendous expenditures. We are all very much concerned with the burden that our people have to carry by paying taxes to maintain it; but I say here definitely now, irrespective of anybody else's opinion, we cannot afford to spend less. We have vast areas to defend, and we have a small population. As I pointed out a moment ago, we are vulnerable. Not only are we vulnerable in the air, but on the sea. And the first duty of this government is the protection of its people. Although I regret the heavy expenditure, I say this, and I say it emphatically: We cannot help ourselves. Until such time as international tension eases we have to spend this money if our people are going to get the defence to which they are entitled.
I have no criticism of the Department of National Defence. Mistakes have been made; we all know that, but they are not vital mistakes. I have every confidence in the Department of National Defence and in the heads of the three services that they are doing everything possible to give us the defence which we need. But they have a tremendous problem. We have a vast area to defend, and we have to plan for defence
Supply-National Defence with a small population to carry it out, and with limited means. Therefore they have to plan in accordance with the problem as I stated it a moment ago, and it is no easy job. It is a difficult situation. Nobody knows what is going to happen next month or six months hence.
It has been mentioned here that it looks as if we are going to fight the next war as if it were a continuation of the last war. I do not know. The H-bomb has made a difference in our weapons; there is no doubt about that. There is no doubt that some of the weapons we have today will be obsolete. That is a problem that you have to face. And you get different opinions from the highest authorities. Until they have settled that it will be useless for us to spend vast amounts of money unless we know where we are going and why we are spending it.
I have nothing further to say, Mr. Chairman, except that I regret this emergency and I regret our having to spend this money on defence when it could be used for more useful purposes in the world. But while this threat is hanging over our heads-and it is not lessening; Geneva and Indo-China will tell you that-while this threat is there, we shall have to face it if we are to get the protection which we need. I think if the Canadian people, whom I believe to be the finest people on earth, second to none, are told the true hard facts they will face up to them as they have in the past, they will come through as they have in the past, and they will come through no matter what happens.
