speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to follow the arguments which have been advanced by the hon. members who preceded me, nor to repeat the arguments which have been placed before the committee by other members. I was impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West when, apparently in consequence of the words of optimism expressed by the minister yesterday, he pleaded for a reduction in the amount of expenditure for national defence.
The minister gave the house a very complete outline of the situation which, together with the white paper, revealed in some detail Canada's position. But I think the minister went rather far when he gave expression to the following:
It is very risky for people charged with defence to make a prophecy. All we can do is to give opinions and not give assurances, but this system of defence against air attack has reached the stage today where if I were in charge of the Russian air force and were aiming to reach important targets in the United States I would not go across the lines of these radar defences. I would go some other wav. and there are other ways.

Supply-National Defence
That statement, Mr. Chairman, has much in common with the Maginot-line complex of 1935 to 1939 and, having regard to what knowledge one may obtain by visiting various parts of northern Canada, to say the least it is based upon pious optimism. All of us hope that the minister's prophecy may be attained, but it does indicate an attitude of unreality and a failure to appreciate what I think the people of Canada must realize, namely that the danger to our survival is today as great as, if not greater than, it has been since 1945.
The hon. member for Kootenay West urged the establishment of a committee to investigate expenditures to ensure economic expenditure. All hon. members want economic expenditures, but I personally do not see

and I speak for myself alone based on my experience in this house-how such a committee having regard to its party complex can achieve what the people of Canada expect, namely actual production of armaments instead of a march of statistics based upon the amount of expenditures. With some Canadians already weary of the heavy expenditures and heavy taxation it is time our people were made fully aware of the dangers inherent in the world situation.
Recently I had the privilege of seeing something of the situation in Europe at first hand, and in this connection I would like to say that I was given every assistance by the departments of external affairs and defence. I had the privilege of an interview with General Gruenther, a man of masterful personality, tremendous capacity for leadership and with a knowledge of world events which fits him for the position he now occupies. I do not think those associated with him at SHAPE headquarters would express the hope that the danger is less than it was at any time during the last nine years.
Indeed, one of the greatest fears we face today is this, that nations will weary in welldoing and that the continued preparations for war will cause the feeling of apathy which, as one listens to the debate in this house, is not unrevealed in this chamber, if one can draw any conclusion on the basis of the attendance for this debate.
General Gruenther is coming to Canada early in June. He is a man who could give the Canadian people something of the picture as he sees it, and I hope that some time during his two-day visit he will be given the opportunity through the medium of the C.B.C. to place before the Canadian people the defence picture as he can reveal it from his position as supreme commander.
All of us hope for a reduction in war expenditure. We have the right to expect


that the government will institute what it has not heretofore instituted, namely a more meticulous and careful examination of expenditures so that unnecessary and wasteful expenditure will be abolished and the purchase of obsolete weapons will be discontinued.
The minister in his speech revealed a change in his thinking. I well remember some five or six years ago when his emphasis was not upon air power. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, with his unequalled experience and a knowledge of our problems gained during his progress from the ranks to the post of major general, in the infantry during two world wars, long ago indicated that in his opinion what was necessary was an intensification of air power and a lesser emphasis upon other means of defence. In 1949 he made a speech to that effect in this house and I shall read a portion of that speech. On November 18 of that year he said, as reported at page 1960 of Hansard:
Government policies are revealed in the estimates that are produced.
Then in the next paragraph he continued:
I have been an infantry soldier most of my life and 1 have all the pride and tradition of marching men behind me, but I say with that background that where we are spending under these items $1 on the army we ought to be spending $3 on the air force. One dollar on the army and $3 on the air force. I have not had the advantage of discussing this matter with the committee; 1 have not been able to prepare details of the estimates, but those are the proportions in which the money ought to be spent. That is why I feel in duty bound at this time to oppose the whole policy underlying the maintenance of our forces, because I do not believe the people of Canada are getting the proper amount of protection in return for the money they are providing.
That was his view in 1949. Events since 1949 indicate that his powers of anticipation and prophecy envisaged the world situation of today. The views he then expressed are the views which are accepted now by the general staffs of the various armies. In the British defence white paper of 1954, which to a degree represents the viewpoint of the British chiefs of staff, these words appear:
If by some miscalculation in communist policy or by deliberate design, a global war were to be forced upon us, it must be assumed that atomic weapons would be employed by both sides. In this event, it seems likely that such a war would begin with a period of intense atomic attacks lasting a relatively short time but inflicting great destruction and damage. If no decisive results were reached in this opening phase, hostilities would decline in intensity, though perhaps less so at sea than elsewhere, and a period of "broken-backed" warfare would follow, during which the opposing sides would seek to recover their strength, carrying on the struggle in the meantime as best they might.
Such a prospect emphasizes yet again the prime necessity of basing our defence policy upon the

prevention of war. It also makes clear the need to keep the lead which we now hold in technical development on which we must rely to offset the preponderance of the communist states in manpower.
Then it goes on to say this:
The basic one must be that by 1960-if not already-the Soviet union will be in possession of an ample stock of tactical atomic weapons, and she may strike in a very different manner from the sort of build-up and attack she would have launched in the pre-atomic days.
The views of the British chiefs of staff in 1954 represent in large measure the viewpoint expressed by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich in 1949. The government can learn much of benefit in the discussions in the House of Commons by members with knowledge and a realization of the issues as they are. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, with available atomic weapons, apparently stands in a better position than at any time throughout recent years. We are in a position-and I quote the reference to General Gruenther to which I believe allusion has already been made-where the U.S.S.R. have nothing that would match the B-47 today. But with the expansion taking place in connection with atomic energy in the U.S.S.R., our great danger is that if we fail to continue to produce and to secure the largest possible return for the defence dollar spent, five years from now we shall find ourselves in a position where our relative strength in atomic weapons will be lower as compared with that of the U.S.S.R. One of the great deterrents to war is atomic power. Its influence for peace may be lost within five years because of our failure to place greater emphasis on air development and to spend a greater portion of our defence dollar upon aircraft capable of conveying atomic bombs to their destinations.
I well remember when in 1949 the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich advanced his arguments, on behalf of air power, the answer that was invariably given was in effect that his views did not represent the view of those in authority on the staff.
My friend the hon. member for Kootenay West indicated that some nations are reducing their expenditures. He mentioned the United States and he also referred to Turkey. Those reductions are taking place, not by reducing the amount produced but actually by savings and by economies, thus achieving the same return as the expenditure of the larger amount would have achieved.
I believe every facility should be provided to members of the House of Commons to see at first hand the situation in Europe as it is. I have never advocated junkets at the
Supply-National Defence expense of the state; far from it, but Canadian members of parliament should have the same opportunity that United States members of congress have to see what is going on over there. Such visits should be provided not at the expense, as I say, of the state but by utilizing the facilities that are available as the Royal Canadian Air Force engages in routine flights or other training expeditions. Only by first hand knowledge can members of parliament have a knowledge of conditions.
The minister mentioned the power of NATO. The progress that has taken place in the last three or four years has been tremendous. The results are a tribute to those who have given their devotion to the service of the organization comprising fourteen member nations who have been able to work together in a way that could not have been anticipated a few years ago. But certainly one of the great dangers in NATO is that discord and dissension will take place, similar to the divisions among the free nations as have been revealed in the Geneva conference. Disunity and division, confusion and cleavage. Ultimately disunity will result in the weakening of the western democratic and freedom-loving nations. Failure to agree is playing into the hands of the communists.
Two striking things during my trip come to mind. One was to see in France, a matter of but a few days ago, something of what communism can do. I was in the gallery of the chambre des deputes the day that Dien Bien Phu was captured. The communists there knew what had happened. They forgot the glory of France in their apparent joy at the fact that destruction had come to the French army that had so gallantly defended that outpost in Indo-China. A day later I saw something of the spirit of France when, in defeat, everywhere there was that attitude of mourning and courage which indicated that out of that defeat in Indo-China will come a new determination and a renewed power for greatness.
It has been said that in Europe communism is in recession. The answer is in the returns of the election which took place recently in northern France where the communists won a surprise local victory and the same in Italy where some 30 per cent of the people are voting communist. These things are of interest to us because to the degree that communism is able to establish itself, to that extent the possibility of the European defence community plan being passed and brought into being recedes into the future.

Mr. Chairman, I was dealing in general with the NATO organization, the need of its preservation and the realization by all of us that criticism of other nations within NATO is a detrimental course and weakens that organization at a time that the communists are endeavouring to cause dissension, disorganization, disagreement, delay and deferment of decisions. When we sometimes feel prone to criticize the United States of America let us realize one
[The Deputy Chairman.]
fact, that of the $68 billion this year that is being expended through the NATO organization to maintain and preserve freedom almost 80 per cent is furnished by the United States of America.
The communists' aim and endeavour is to divide, to divide and rule because of the division. They adopt a different policy in every part of Europe to meet the circumstances of the country in which they are. In France they oppose EDC and say in effect that the 500,000 men that Germany would provide are unnecessary. They go back to the hundreds of years of difference and difficulty between France and Germany. In Italy they bring up the question of Trieste and contend that if EDC is ratified by Italy then in that case the hope of the Italians to retrieve Trieste will be gone.
In northern Italy they operate in the trade unions on the basis that they have achieved a great deal for the workmen. Among the farmers they say that there will be no rent. For every area they have a policy. Their purpose is to divide and thereby destroy the security which the unity of NATO alone can preserve. I hope that everything will be done by our leaders to bring home to the Canadian people and to the peoples of all the nations within the NATO organization the imperative need of preservation of the unity of NATO. Unity cannot be divisible and freedom survive.
Next, the maintenance of the spiritual things of free men is important. In that regard I think the recent judgment of the supreme court of the United States denying segregation is one of the greatest steps forward for democracy everywhere in the world in removing as it will one of those stumbling blocks with which communism has been able to block the roadway to freedom for the coloured races. I predict that magnificent judgment will take its place internationally in the years ahead in the struggle against communism to the same degree as Lincoln's emancipation declaration had its effective results in unifying the various states of the United States.
NATO is a tremendous project. Canada has made a worthy contribution. I bring you from among the NATO nations a message of the appreciation of the contribution of Dana Wilgress and those associated with him. I believe that if there had been a similar organization during the 1930's a second world war might have been averted. What NATO has done is to build a shield in Europe that could not have been foreseen two or three years ago.
The NATO nations possess 5,800 aircraft, of which 2,400 are jet fighters. In addition,

they have a thousand more based in Great Britain. Throughout Europe they have built up airports capable of accommodating 350 jets. They have forces which, while they will not stop the enemy if it moves, will nonetheless act as a deterrent. There are 500,000 on the German front compared with 400,000 in the armies immediately opposite them. Across Europe from West Germany to Turkey NATO today has 3,100,000 men under arms compared with 4 million in the Soviet.
NATO is doing something more. It is organizing the economic strength of these nations. NATO nations have 68 per cent of the oil in Europe, 76 per cent of the shipping, 66 per cent of the steel, 59 per cent of the coal and 62 per cent of the electric power. This has been achieved because there has been unity. I fear that the unity that built this great alliance for defence and survival is in danger of being broken by the disagreements that are taking place at Geneva and elsewhere. Divisions among the free nations help the communists. I believe that above everything else we of the freedom-loving parliaments must take a firm stand against unnecessary divisions, disagreements or cleavages among the free nations. We must realize that only in unity is there survival.
What can NATO do in Canada? One of its programs is called infrastructure. I do not know who invented that strangely sounding word. Under infrastructure NATO builds airfields, communication lines, oil pipe lines and so on. Accepting the general thesis, now accepted by the minister and rather disavowed five years ago, that the major element in our defence is air power, I believe that the nations of NATO and in particular the United States, in view of the fact she is our closest neighbour and realizes our vast mineral resources that are so necessary for the survival of NATO, should give consideration to assistance in building strategic roads within this country that are necessary to defence. Such roads, besides being of great defence value, would be useful at the present time in order to provide a means of ingress and egress of our northern areas.
The opposition of the minister has been expressed on a number of occasions, but he has changed his mind on the question of the need for the intensification of air development. His attitude in the past has been opposed to doing anything in this regard. Having regard to the position in the western provinces, the oil, uranium and other minerals there, I believe our present roadway situation is such that in the event of war many of these strategic needs would be denied to our forces. I believe that there
Supply-National Defence should be not only defence highways into the north, useful in time of war and in particular to provide a means of securing these necessary muniments of war such as uranium and oil, but additional to the trans-Canada highway a defence highway in the north is necessary through the Yellowhead pass. This suggestion is supported by the people of northern Saskatchewan and Alberta, and also by those living in the southernmost parts of these two provinces. The Edmonton Journal of April 29 set forth the situation regarding the Yellowhead highway in these words:
This much at least must be said for defence minister Brooke Claxton's attitude to the Yellowhead highway project, as displayed on his visit here this week; he does not beat about the bush. Questioned about the possibility of building the road as a defence measure, he stated that it would serve no useful military purpose. An attack on Canada in a future war, he predicted, would be by air, and highways would not be involved in the defence.
If one goes back to 1946 and 1947 and reads some of the speeches made by the ministers of this government at that time, one finds that the possibility of attack by air, now accepted as a possibility, was ridiculed and the need for the establishment of radar stations in northern Canada to effectively meet that danger potentiality was frowned upon.
Then, the editorial says this:
This will strike most westerners as a rash and hasty judgment. Under modem conditions, an enemy may well choose to attack Canada, and especially its northwestern regions, by air. But the repulse of such an attack may depend in large measure on speedy and reliable ground transportation, for instance in the case of bad flying weather. Then, again, the Calgary Albertan dealt with the situation in an editorial of May 6 in these words:
When defence minister Claxton was in Edmonton a few days ago, he said that a first-class highway through the Yellowhead pass, affording direct connection between Vancouver and Edmonton, would serve no useful military purpose. The Edmonton Journal, tireless advocate of the Yellowhead route, took Mr. Claxton to task for that statement, and with justification.
The Calgary newspaper gives its support to this highway and to northern highways in general as part of our defence project. Speaking as a member from the province of Saskatchewan I say that today our situation is such, with the location of uranium and the potentialities of Beaverlodge in northern Saskatchewan, that all that vast area might well be lost to our defence effort unless something in the nature of a defence highway is provided. Indeed, a military man and scientist, Dr. Mawdsley of the University of

Then I come to one other matter in connection with NATO. One cannot separate the defence sections in NATO from those dealing with economic development. I am one of those who fear that you cannot hold an organization like NATO together by the simple expedient of continuing fear. They-

-will seek to eliminate conflict in their international economic policies, and will encourage economic collaboration between any or all of them.

These are but a few matters that have occurred to me, that I felt I could bring to the attention of the committee on this occasion. We will not preserve our freedom, we will not preserve our security, simply by vast statistics of expenditures without there being for those expenditures the best possible use made of the money expended. There will not be a building up of unity within NATO unless there is economic co-operation as yet nonexistent. There will not be available to NATO the vast resources of northern Canada unless and until the Department of National Defence realizes that highways north and south into those areas, which otherwise will not have such highways, are made available. In the event of war or attack through the north polar areas, or over the ice cap, we must be in a position to make available to our armed forces and to those of the other nations in NATO the vast resources of northern Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not take much of the time of the committee but I would like to refer briefly to what was said by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, and also just now by the hon. member for Prince Albert. In emphasizing the need for highways as a means of defence I would not have risen at this time had it not been for the fact that I think it is vitally important that great emphasis be placed upon defence highways in Canada. I believe those highways are absolutely necessary for the protection of our people, and as vitally needed as any other form of protection. I think of the Vancouver area and of the one bridge leading out of that city. I think of the many thousands of people who, as it were, would be cooped up without any way of getting out of the city because of a lack of highways and bridges.
It is time our government took a realistic view of what is needed by way of highways. It is time the government took another look, because in travelling across this country I have found that many people are becoming greatly concerned about the civil defence situation. Co-operation between the Department of National Defence and the civil defence authorities is an absolute must. Furthermore, certain civilian highways now in existence are inadequate.
Any expenditures made by the Department of National Defence in the building of highways would bring about something of a permanent nature which, in time to come, would be of real value to the people of Canada, and certainly would not, as occurs in so many cases, be lost to the civilian cause.
National highways for purposes of defence are fast becoming a national issue because the people are alarmed. It is only reasonable to expect that they would become alarmed- although perhaps the minister would not agree when I say they are. However I do travel around in various parts of the country and find that this subject is continually on their tongues and in their conversation. They point out that nothing is being done in the building of highways for purposes of defence.
Looking at the minister's speech as it is reported in Hansard, and particularly at the figures he placed on record, I note that more than $850 million has been spent for industrial equipment. Surely, looking at the over-all picture, in the light of that great expenditure for industrial equipment there must be some place in the plan of things whereby we can reach a balance and have some moneys allocated to the building of defence highways. I make this reference, Mr. Chairman, only for purposes of emphasis, and because I think it is very important.

Mr. Chairman, it is with a certain amount of timidity I rise to speak on a subject involving an expenditure of $1,902,823,500. Before coming to the House of Commons I thought that was a lot of money; but if I am to judge by the lack of concern of hon. members as indicated by the slim attendance in the house today perhaps the time will come when I will not consider this a large sum of money.
The fact is however that the amount I have indicated does constitute two-fifths of the budget for this country. I have been advised that if I inquire too closely as to how the money is spent I will be advised, in reply to certain questions, that it is not in the national interest to disclose the way those moneys are spent. It is for this reason I rise to point out to the committee that for any government of Canada, representing the percentage of population of the western democracies it does represent, as indicated by the vote of the electors, to suggest it has any secrets, the divulgence of which would have an adverse effect upon the forces of the western democracies is very close to ridiculous.
May I say with vigour that I am in wholehearted accord with every suggestion made in the house that a committee should be formed, or some other steps taken, to allow individual members to familiarize themselves with what is received in kind for the dollars and cents actually spent. We must not be content with merely a statement by a minister who expresses an opinion on information received, or something of that nature. As a member of the house I do not even know the source of the information on which his opinion is based.
With respect to this Gargantua in our midst, this defence spending, let me say I do not believe there is a taxpayer in Canada who is not prepared to spend his or her fair share for purposes of defence. I make that statement without qualification. But there is also an onus on the Department of National Defence to see that money is not spent needlessly, or that it is not taken unnecessarily from the taxpayers.
I suggest there are certain assets standing in the name of the Department of National Defence which are not serving the defensive system in our country. At one time they did serve the defence of the country and served it well. At the present time they do not. I refer to the fixed assets. One in particular to which I refer is the Long Branch rifle range. This property is situated in the township of Toronto, in the county of Peel. At one time perhaps it was used extensively as a rifle range and may have had some particular purpose. I am quite familiar with the area. It comprises several hundred acres
Supply-National Defence of land and is a sort of luxury gift to be used by certain non-permanent units a very few days in the year. It could now be used by the taxpayers of the municipality of the township of Toronto to bring in large industrial assessments which in turn would lighten the tax load of the taxpayers. Representations have been made over the years to the Department of National Defence to release these lands, and as of the date of my making this speech no action has been taken by the Department of National Defence to release those lands. I suggest to the minister that in all fairness to the taxpayers of the area this is an example of the Department of National Defence holding an expensive asset for no particular purpose.
The argument has been advanced that it is really for a rifle range. When one compares the distance from Toronto of the area when it was first created in relation to the method of transportation then in existence I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that Camp Borden is as close to Toronto today to fill all the purposes for which this rifle range might be used, and that the land should be released.
As to other matters affecting the Department of National Defence, I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the minister might well concern himself with his program of advertising pensions. The average person who enlists in the navy, army or air force is probably concerned with the fact that a pension is offered. The minister may say that pensions are not his particular responsibility. Since they deal with the people whom he is hiring I suggest to him that they are in his department, and when I refer to him the treatment which his people and the widows of his people are receiving, he will observe the unfairness of the situation where no pension is received when death or accident is not due to service, although actually the individual is in service. The pension that is given, or rather not given, is, I suggest to the minister, creating a very definite hardship.
I refer particularly to a very recent example of Flying Officer Joseph Goldthorpe, who enlisted in 1940 and served with distinction in the Royal Canadian Air Force for five years. After the war he endeavoured to re-enlist in the air force, but I understand he was advised that he would have to reduce his rank. He enlisted in the Royal Air Force and was offered a permanent commission. Through good fortune, the Royal Canadian Air Force was able to secure him. He came back and re-enlisted in the Royal Canadian Air Force. I say to the minister that this flying officer, with distinguished service, died

Supply-National Defence one day at noon in the officers' mess. He was buried with full air force honours in North Bay, and his widow received the magnificent contribution in gratia of $100. I suggest to the minister that he might well consider the pension plan set forth in the advertisements and dispose of the pension suggestion in the advertisements because they are not all one might gather from reading them and people are being misled.
While we are dealing with advertisements I would refer the minister to an advertisement which appeared in this morning's Globe and Mail of Toronto, which I understand is fairly widely read in that area. It contains an advertisement of guardsmen marching, and the following:
Applications now being accepted for the new Regiment of Canadian Guards.
I have great pride in the name "guard". I had the honour of serving in a guards regiment during the war myself. I suggest to the minister that the advertisement is misleading in that it is an advertisement of guards and in the small print says:
Canadian guards qualifications may be obtained from any recruiting officer.
I suggest to the minister that perhaps he has not complete knowledge of the advertisement. It is to get people into the recruiting office under false pretences. They publish a nice advertisement and then they refer to the special qualifications of the guards in the righthand corner. I would ask the minister to deal with it later on in his remarks and tell us whether it is the intention of the Department of National Defence to discontinue the great tradition which put the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery on the right of the line and then the armoured corps next, and so on down the units; or is the suggestion in this advertisement that the guards will be second to none on the parade ground misleading, because as I understand the expression "second to none on the parade ground" means that you are on the right of the line. Is it the suggestion of the Department of National Defence that this Regiment of Canadian Guards shall be on the right of the line, or shall the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery and the armoured corps continue to occupy this position? It is a fair question to ask because it is causing quite a bit of concern to many people who are affiliated with those regiments.
In connection with the billeting of married men in married quarters in places such as ordnance depots and the like, I am advised that pressure is being brought to bear by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation with respect to financing builders of rental units that they must allocate certain units

to service personnel, or that before they will finance certain individual houses they require the builders to build certain apartment houses. In certain municipalities this will cause great hardship. The minister in his speech yesterday at page 4909 of Hansard said:
In the United States last year, one-third of the entire strength of the United States armed forces were separated from the forces last year. In Canada the equivalent figure was about one-seventh. We want to maintain our rates of reengagement: we want to increase it if we can, but to say that it is a grave problem is a gross exaggeration.
In fairness the minister should have continued to say that the bulk of the service personnel in the United States armed forces are draftees, and that the one-third who are leaving the army are merely leaving it at the expiration of the draft period. I would ask the minister if a better comparison would not be to give the numbers leaving the United States army who are volunteers, as compared with the figure in the Canadian army, which is a completely volunteer army. I should now like to deal briefly with the problem of civil defence. It is a problem that the minister mentioned. At the outset I would say that the minister should either tell us that there is a threat or there is not, because civil defence in this country seems to be something patterned on the "after you, Alphonse" system. People are trying to throw the responsibility on others. I think that initiative and leadership must be shown. The Department of National Defence means exactly what it says, and I suggest to the minister that civil defence is a matter worthy of his very serious consideration. As he said himself yesterday, it does little to train troops for overseas if civil defence is not properly taken care of.
In that regard I would suggest to the minister that he should make a very careful reconsideration of what I suspect is his

attitude toward the reserve army in Canada. During the last war-and before that, of course, though I will confine my remarks to the present time-the reserve army units were very highly commended. In fact they actually produced a general, and I refer to the general commanding the fifth division in which I served. He was from the reserve army. The reserve army units responded tremendously upon the outbreak of the Korean war. They were given certain allocations and they filled every one of them.
I would suggest to the minister that he attend some evening parades of the reserve army and he will find that with very few exceptions-and I say with pride that one of these exceptions is the Lome Scots regiment which is the regiment from my own sounty-the officers on parade outnumber the N.C.O.'s and enlisted men. If the minister wishes to accept that suggestion then perhaps it would be better if he gave no notice of his intention but just dropped in to say "Hello".

They will be required for military duties, policing, and other duties following air raids and they will be the only force immediately available for such tasks. In view of that I would suggest that the minister should take that fact into consideration in his estimates, and make an honest effort to rejuvenate the reserve army.

But we have not got all that we planned for that expenditure.
In the final sentence I quoted originally the minister did not say nine-tenths or
Supply-National Defence seventeen-twentieths. He said "more than four-fifths" so I take it that that is the closest figure. The minister's estimate for the entire program was $5 billion but I would suggest in the light of these figures that the minister has made a billion dollar error at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer. Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the thing that must impress itself most on the mind of any hon. member who has been in this house, and certainly on anyone who has come into the galleries this afternoon, is the spirit of utter unreality in which the material survival of Canada is being discussed. At 3.40 this afternoon, at a time when we were discussing the expenditure of $2 billion in a single year and, far more important than that, the means by which we can defend our freedom, there were 11 Liberal members in the house and not a single cabinet minister.
There are not many Conservatives here now.
How many were there on your side of the house?

Mr. Chairman, there have not been many on either side of the house and the reason is because of the soporific speech by the minister which left the impression that we are in a satisfactory state in the defence of this country after having spent more than $5 billion. We must measure that in terms of what we have in reality.
We have been told of the fighter squadrons in Europe. Those squadrons are well equipped, well trained and unquestionably equal to any that are ready for service in that area. We know of the standard of excellence of the members of the armed forces, the infantry, artillery and other branches of the service which have been in Korea and which are there now. We know of the high level of training in the permanent units.
Nevertheless, that is the only final product of the whole defence plan of Canada. It might well be that if we were drifting along in a period of easy assurance and there was no danger of war we could look with some measure of satisfaction, with some measure of complacency at the actual situation in which the reserve forces of this country now find themselves. Every hon. member in this house who has followed the debates, and most certainly every hon. member who has served in one of the armed forces, knows that the reserve units are the backbone of Canadian defence. No one will question that,

Supply-National Defence least of all the Minister of National Defence. Therefore, as we examine our position, as we come close to four years since the outbreak of a very real and very deadly war in Korea, let us see with just what measure of reality we have brought our reserve units up to a position in which they could occupy the field if that dreadful necessity arose.
Either in a direct capacity or some other capacity I have been associated with the reserve forces of Canada since 1910. That is a long time. I say without any hesitation that in spite of the improvement of equipment and things of that kind the reserve units of this country are less able to go into the field today in the event of an emergency than they have been at any time within that 40 years.
Just a moment ago the hon. member for Peel in his speech, and an excellent speech it was, placed before the house the dreadful warning that is to be found in the unchallengeable fact that in many parts of this country, where units with long historic pasts gather to train, there are more officers on parade than other ranks. That illustrates a condition which is behind the statement I have just made with regard to the readiness of reserve units to be mobilized and to be employed.
Let us go back to the days of the first world war. For some that is almost getting back to the Crimea. Nevertheless for some of us those days are still very fresh and real. Just prior to that war the reserve units went into camp at close to full strength, whether they were infantry, artillery, cavalry or other branches of the service. That year I saw infantry units that were well up to the full authorized establishment for camp. That year I saw artillery units some of whose men had to be paid from the pockets of the officers because they had more than were authorized. That is something that happened on other occasions.
Those units were horse units; they were artillery units. They moved their own guns and they moved complete complements of guns. They took them to camp and they carried out their manoeuvres in camp. Infantry units carried out training of a nature that is only possible where you have a complete unit in form. So it was with the cavalry and with other branches of the service at that time. War broke upon the world with a suddenness far more unexpected than in 1939 when, on August 4, 1914 we were confronted with something utterly unexpected at that time by people who had basked in the sunshine of peace for so long. Nevertheless, although that situation arose unexpectedly, less than eight weeks after the sudden outbreak of war the first Canadian division sailed


for Britain ready to take their part. I grant you that there were long months of training before they went into the field, but it was not so many months later that those men, who had left Canada less than two months after that sudden outbreak of war, were taking their place against the most highly trained troops the world had known up to that time.
Another war came. There was not the comparative readiness then, although the equipment had advanced so much. Not by any manner of means were the units as ready as they were in 1914, in comparison to their needs. Nevertheless most batteries of artillery, infantry units, cavalry units and other units of the reserve forces had equipment that could be used for training immediately.
Now let us see where we are at after having spent some $5| billion. Let us see where we are at almost four years after the outbreak of another real war, namely that in Korea. Let us see exactly with what reality the reserve forces have been prepared to be the backbone of our defence. Mr. Chairman, the situation is rather similar in many cases; but let me deal with one branch of the service. What is substantially true there is substantially true in a great many other cases.
Last year at Petawawa-the great artillery camp not so far from here-one of the groups of artillery, that had one of the best firing records last year, consisted of two medium regiments of artillery and five field regiments. That group, which was rated fairly highly, was probably at best at about one-quarter of the strength that was actually authorized. When it comes to the firing that was done- and that was after more than three years had elapsed since the outbreak of war in Korea- may I say that the five field regiments of that particular group that were in camp at the same time at Petawawa last year fired 24 guns instead of the 120 guns authorized for the number of batteries that would be included in that group. This year at best, those five regiments amongst the better regiments in this country at the present time will perhaps fire 28 guns instead of the 120 guns which would be the number of guns fired by five regiments according to their ordinary strength. Last year the total number of guns fired by five regiments was exactly the number of guns alloted to a single regiment up to strength.
Then when it comes to these units going to camp this year, only one of those regiments will have two batteries, although regimental strength is three. The rest will have only one battery and in most cases only a single troop of guns. That, Mr. Chairman, is the

state of readiness of one of the better groups of artillery of the reserve force at this time.
Last night, in one of the most accurate and comprehensive descriptions I have heard of the position of the armoured forces, and given to this committee by a gallant officer of the armoured corps, we were told of the ineffectiveness of the armoured training at this time. We know that the same thing is true with regard to the most historic infantry units. This is the situation in which we now find ourselves after the expenditure of this enormous sum of money. We are therefore confronted with the fact that it is not dollars that count, Mr. Chairman, it is what we have obtained for them. The time has now come for everyone to ask, in more detail than has been given, what has happened to that money and why it is that we have not obtained better results for what we have spent.

Mr. Chairman, the subject that we have been discussing is one that transcends all others in importance both as far as the money and the result of the expenditure of that money are concerned. In a large measure members of this house must be called upon to bear responsibility for what is or is not accomplished as the result of that expenditure. In some substantial measure we are in the same position as a board of directors representing shareholders who are the people of Canada. Of course we are dealing with something far more important, far larger in its significance and more far-reaching in its ultimate consequences than any board of directors can ever be called upon to deal with. I mention that particularly because the management in this case have sought the advice of certain experts regarding the organization and effectiveness of the reserve forces. Three very competent officers of long experience were called upon to examine the situation and to make their recommendations. It 83276-315

It is largely because of the withholding of reports and information of this kind and the withholding of basic facts which are essential to the satisfactory discussion of this

When I spoke this afternoon of the small numbers on both sides of the house attending the debate I was not forgetful of the fact that important committees are sitting and that many hon. members were attending committee meetings. The very fact that I am called upon to mention that emphasizes one of the reasons why the discussion of these important subjects in the house is so unsatisfactory. Important committees are delayed until the very last minute. We only started a few days ago to deal with veterans affairs although we have been sitting since last November. Even now there is still extremely important legislation to come forward. Members are called upon to attend these committee meetings and generally the whole atmosphere is such that for those members who are concerned about this subject there is great difficulty in finding the time to attend the discussions which should take place and which should be listened to here in the house.
It was not because of any lack of interest, Mr. Chairman, or positive suggestion in the speeches that were made that there was any atmosphere of unreality. The member for Esquimalt-Saanich yesterday made one of the best speeches on national defence that has been made in this house, since I came here, at any rate. The hon. member who made that speech is the best qualified officer in Canada to make a speech of that kind. He is a man who has been through every rank in the army from private to major general, from carrying a rifle in the rear ranks to the command of a division, and after that to the Pacific coast command during the last war.
Speak up so the general can hear you.

The comment that is made, of course, would display something of which the hon. member who interrupted would not be aware, that is that he may have some modesty. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich has had an experience which qualifies him to make a statement in this house about national defence in a way that is not equalled by any member on either side of the house. When he speaks of training for battle, and the needs of battle, he speaks as an officer with unequalled experience in battle. Other officers have made similar contributions, officers who are now members of this house.
Nor have these speeches been confined to those in the officer rank, by any manner of means. We have heard speeches from those who served in other ranks, and in doing so


that, no matter how much we may respect the earnestness of the minister in relation to his responsibilities, we have to take his statements at their face value. His statements at their face value give us very little real information, give us very little of practical value in relation to the problem we are called upon to judge at this time. Let us remember that it is the private members on both sides of the house whose responsibility is represented in the request for some $2 billion for national defence in the current fiscal year.
Let the minister tell us what has gone wrong instead of telling us that everything is the best in the world, or imitating the very famous literary expression, that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds. Let him tell us why there has been this inability to get the reserve forces up to a level where they could be mobilized in the event of hostilities. Let him tell us why it is that the equipment is not adequate. Let him answer the question that has been raised in regard to the armoured forces, in regard to the infantry, in regard to the other units which are short of equipment at this time. We will be ready to listen to that; we are not ready to be told that all is well when we know all is not well.
No matter what might have been possible two weeks ago, Mr. Chairman, the loss of Dien Bien Phu ushered in a new period of military appreciation. Whatever may have been valid before that is not valid today unless it is examined in the light of that experience. Brave, well equipped, well trained units were overrun in a fortress that had been prepared with great care. I have no doubt every hon. member heard the description of the bombardment which preceded the final overrunning of that fortress. Those who were there in that earlier experience said that there had not been any barrage like it since the drumfire of Verdun.
That is the kind of thing that has emerged in this distant jungle and in these plains in distant points throughout the world, where Russian guns in the hands of Chinese troops moved from Korea after the armistice now mass their strength against the scattered outposts of the western world. That is the reality we face, and we must face it in terms of cold reality. We must reassess our position. We must examine the kind of forces that are needed to meet that kind of situation. Do we believe for one moment that we are going to meet manpower with manpower on the plains of Europe, if the necessity should come to meet the teeming millions of Russia? I do not think that anyone does. We know perfectly well that under no circumstances

can the western world mass forces in the distant jungles and plains of Asia on equal terms.
These call for a new assessment; these call for a new type of organization; certainly, at least they call for the examination of that possibility. Those who remember what happened in Burma during the last war will recall the successful unconventional forces that were organized to fight a different type of enemy through the jungle with great success. Is that the kind of force we need? Instead of heavily equipped paratroops, do we perhaps need some new type of very informal mobile force? We do not know unless the discussion is opened up, with all the information available to us that is available to the government. Certainly the only thing that will give comfort to the enemy is our failure to examine these things in terms of stern reality.
We have another problem before us in Canada. We are the third largest country in the world with fifteen million people. What kind of armed force do we need that will be most effective both in this large area and for overseas service? We have a navy, a well trained navy; we have highly trained and well equipped air units in the permanent units of the R.C.A.F.; we have excellent infantry units in the permanent branch of the service. I repeat, our reserve units are keen and anxious to do their job, but are severely limited both by numbers, by equipment and by the opportunities for training under those circumstances. What do we need? I merely put this forward as a suggestion, but it is one of the things that would be put forward if we were really able to have the recommendation before us that have been made and other recommendations as well.
Is it not possible that we should concentrate entirely on air units of different kinds, except for fairly limited naval and other units? Is it not possible that we should have all our artillery, all our armoured forces, all our reconnaissance forces, all the engineers and all the other forces-we are not including the medical forces-airborne ready to be moved by air transport to any distant point? Certainly that would be the thing that would be most effective to meet a possible threat to this country, and it certainly would be the thing that would be most effective to make our strength felt at distant points throughout the world. I do not put this forward as any dogmatic suggestion; I merely say it is one of the kind of things that should be considered as an alternative to the continuous training of units that are essential segments of the old type of continental force.

We are still training with the same mentality we had when we believed that our units were going to be parts of divisions and army formations in Europe or in some other great mainland, but particularly Europe. Let us with all the ingenuity we have-and we are an ingenious people-devise the kind of force that will be best for Canada and at the same time serve our purpose within the framework of NATO and of the other organizations. Probably there are hon. members who have read the most interesting and illuminating book of all time-I hope they have all read it-under the title "The Reason Why" based upon that classic poem:
Theirs not to reason why,
Theirs but to do and die.
Well, anybody who is prepared to accept the proposition that it is not for hon. members to reason why, but just to accept the statement of the government, and particularly the Department of National Defence, should read "The Reason Why" and find the reason why we should accept nothing but full information in regard to every aspect of defence here in this country.
The minister spoke of civil defence. It is appropriate that he should speak about civil defence because that is the department under which it should be. Since he spoke on that let us see what he says, as reported at page 4906 of Hansard:
There has been some tendency by some people here and elsewhere to take the view that the destructive power of the H-bomb makes civil defence measures futile. Nothing could be further from the truth.
Then, a few sentences later he said:
Our plans must continue to receive the closest examination in the light of all the circumstances, but the planning and oganization of civil defence measures must be pressed forward.
I refer to that because I make this recommendation to the Prime Minister tonight, as I have this opportunity to do in the committee. Civil defence can no longer be regarded as something remote from national defence generally. We had a statement about three weeks ago by the Minister of National Health and Welfare that this subject is now too serious to permit any argument as to whether this is a problem for the national government, the provincial governments or the municipalities. Certainly it is. The H-bomb, which may embrace in its destructive power several communities, has rendered meaningless this division of responsibility, and what the Minister of National Health and Welfare said should leave no doubt that the government should now transfer this subject to the Department of National Defence and bring the whole matter of civil defence under the government here in Ottawa.

The municipalities simply cannot accept the financial responsibility of preparing themselves for this effort. I agree completely, and agree with the utmost earnestness, with what the minister said that under no circumstances should we accept the proposition that these frightful weapons have now rendered civil defence measures futile.
Who knows where the outlying limits of the destructive area of a new bomb of that kind would be? It might only partly encroach upon any municipality, but the municipality which did not prepare for destruction of that kind would simply find people uncared for and no plans made for their removal, for their care, and for their medical treatment. The greater the area of destruction the greater the need for civil defence and the greater the need for a unified command, and for a centralized authority over something that is of national concern.
Arguing as I so frequently do the importance of the decentralization of authority in regard to local affairs, I believe implicitly that national defence is a strictly national affair and civil defence, as part of national defence, should be under the government here at Ottawa and financed by the dominion treasury.
The need for a recognition of what has been said by the Minister of National Defence is all too apparent, Mr. Chairman, and I hope that the government will take heed of what he has said and what has been said by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. This is a subject which cannot be left where it is. One day we were told there was an agreement on a broad scale with the provinces and next day we had a statement from the minister responsible in Ontario to the effect that there was no agreement at all.
I hope no one will say they are not particularly interested in civil defence in Ontario. After all, Ontario has close to a third of the population of Canada and it does so happen that the number of other provinces, which bring up the total to a majority of the population of Canada, have not entered into any agreement. Surely this cannot be a satisfactory situation in the face of this threat. Surely there can be no better way of meeting whatever was said by the Minister of National Defence, or the emphasis placed upon this subject by the Minister of Health and Welfare, than to change the pattern and bring this within the authority of this department, and to integrate these activities with other activities and other branches of the service where undoubtedly there could be a greater economy in the use of their forces, and undoubtedly the medical 

services of the army, navy and air force could be embraced in new plans for civil defence.
Then, Mr. Chairman, there is the question of the whole approach to the items that are going to come before us. Any hon. member who looks at the large figures embracing the entire military service will realize how impossible it is to go into these details.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have been critical, and critical particularly of the complacent suggestion that has been made that all is well. All is not well; all is far from well. Ask any member of the conference of defence associations which met here in Ottawa during the past winter if all is well. They will tell you what the finding of that conference was. Ask any member who has attended the annual meetings of the artillery association, infantry association, the engineers' association, the signals association, or any other military association if all is well, and they will tell you it is not. They have been making vigorous and repeated recommendations.
Having said that, I say without any hesitation that the minister will find us anxious to co-operate and anxious to offer any encouragement we can. But after all why should that encouragement not be given, because most of these hon. members who have already spoken on this subject are men who have themselves had reason to know the importance of adequate equipment and adequate training on the field of battle.
The test of that co-operation, the test of our ability to unite behind a vigorous national effort which embraces an all-understood foreign policy and an all-understood defence policy would depend entirely upon the extent to which we are taken into the confidence of the government. Let the government appoint a committee of inquiry similar to the Currie committee to make an all-embracing report in regard to the army organization and to see how our dollars can best be used. Such a committee need not decide policy. But in so far as policy is concerned let us have the report of the three officers who inquired into the situation affecting the reserve forces; let us have any other recommendations in the possession of the government; and then this government will find us ready to go out along the highroads and byroads to any part of this country and be just as vigorous as any government would want anyone to be in the build-up of the defence of Canada with full knowledge of what the facts actually are.

speechtext: Order. I think the time has come when I should perhaps remind the committee that at the moment the Minister of National Defence has the floor. We have endeavoured to see that those who were speaking previously in this debate were not interrupted without their consent. We shall expect the same treatment for the Minister of National Defence.
Let him be accurate, Mr. Chairman.

I would not have referred to these rather minor things had they not been referred to by somebody else.
At the beginning of his speech the Leader of the Opposition referred, in terms which were eloquent and fair, to the work of the permanent forces. I have not a full note of what he said because time has not permitted me to get Hansard, but he said that our fighters in Europe were unquestionably equal to any, and that the state of the infantry was excellent. He referred to the high level of training of the permanent force. Then he made a most curious remark when he said "That only is the final product". What kind of product do you want except something that is unquestionably equal to any, is excellent, and has a high level of training? That being the objective of our defence effort, to have it recognized by the Leader of the Opposition-as it must be recognized because it is true-I must say will give great satisfaction to the officers and men who have done the job.
Then the Leader of the Opposition went on and dealt with the actual situation of the reserve forces and made a number of remarks that I shall not examine in detail at this time. But at the end he asked this question: Why is the reserve not up to strength? It has never been planned in the history of Canada that the reserve army should be up to strength. That is not its purpose. It has never had any such program. The fact is that at the present time the strength of the three reserve forces is about 57,000, a figure which is the highest it has ever been in a full year of peacetime.

That statement is not correct. The reserve units have often been up to the full authorized strength.
Oh, oh.
Full authorized strength, as the Leader of the Opposition knows, is not war establishment at all.
Of course it is not. Nobody suggested it was.

I should not like to have the impression left that it was. I am glad that the Leader of the Opposition has not left it that way.
Then as to accommodation, may I say that it has been doubled for the reserve forces. As to equipment, if they lack anything all they have to do is to tell the general officer commanding in the district and he provides it. We have ample equipment of every type needed to train the reserves. The reason why the reserves are not stronger numerically than they are today is plain to see. Whereas at the time when he was an active and good leader of an artillery unit before the war or between the wars, the strength of the active forces was about 8,000 or 9,000 officers and men; and I think one must assume that that figure plus the reserve force included a big proportion of the people in Canada who aimed to have a full-time or part-time service career.
At the present time the strength of the active force is 112,000 and in the active forces today there is a big proportion of the same kind of chap as the Leader of the Opposition and others like myself who, for a time, served in the reserve forces. The reason why they are not in the reserve force is that they are in the active force serving Canada full time. I can perhaps bring that point home by mentioning the fact that from March 31, 1951 to March 31, 1954,-that is just three years-we have taken into the regular permanent force of Canada a total of about 100,000 officers and men. Had we not done so they would have been available for the reserve. As a matter of fact, the reserve has contributed a considerable proportion of that group, just as they should and as they are glad to do. But they cannot help feeling that this fact cuts down their own effective numbers of the most active, keen and interested kind. That is one reason. There may be others.
To look into all of this matter we appointed this committee. As I indicated in my preliminary remarks at the beginning of this debate, when we come to the item dealing with the army reserve I propose to go 

into this matter at greater length or my colleague the Associate Minister of National Defence will do so then.
Mr. Chairman, by that statement do I understand that the minister is going to make the report available at that time?

Oh, no. A report by a board of officials to the chief of the general staff, so far as I know, has never been made available. There is every reason for not making it available. Here there would be every reason for making it available except that it would create the kind of precedent that the Leader of the Opposition and others would make use of in the future. So far as I am concerned, that procedure is not proposed. We propose to make a full report of what is recommended and of what has been done, but the report itself will not be made available because such reports are not made available in this country or in Britain. A minister of national defence, any minister of the crown or any chief of the general staff is entitled to have the confidential advice of a group that he appoints to give him that advice. Unless they can give that advice in confidence, and unless he can take it and act on it or not as he sees fit, we cease to have responsible government.
I shall not go into any of the other matters mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Chairman, because they can be taken up later. I should like to compliment the hon. member for Peel on his maiden speech and to tell him that some of the questions he raised will be mentioned later. He as well as some other hon. members made reference to not having enough information with which to consider these estimates. I have said- without ever having been contradicted, I think-that in this parliament the members have been given, year after year, more information about defence than is given in any other parliament in the British commonwealth.
The minister's saying so does not make it so.

I think the extraordinary thing is that having been given information and not having found what they want- something of a scandalous nature that they could use-they then forget the fact that they have been given information and continue to protest that they have not been given any information. But we have given so much information in the defence expenditure committee meetings, with over forty sessions during three years,

that quite a few hon. members have protested that they are unable to absorb and assimilate the quantity of information they have got.
Another hon. member referred to the fact that he would like to see the product of our defence effort. The product can be seen in Korea, in Germany, in Canada. On every occasion when you see the defence forces you can see the product. That is the kind of thing we are producing, not paper, not words, but trained officers and men equipped and qualified to do the job, and second to none. You know, Mr. Chairman, one of the extraordinary things is that year by year we give opportunities to senators, members of parliament and others to see what is actually going on. We arrange for visits. This year there were visits to the air defence command at St. Hubert, Canadian Vickers Limited, No. 25 central ordnance depot, Canadair Limited, the naval supply depot and to the five major establishments at Kingston, namely, the national defence college, the army staff college, the Royal Military College, the Royal Canadian Electrical and Mechanical Engineers and the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals. Then there was the visit to Churchill, Manitoba.
A total of 129 members of parliament have taken part in a total of 240 visits during this session of parliament, and I have not had one of them report to me anything wrong about anything he saw.
Did he see anything except what you showed him?
I was not on most of the trips.
Or what was showed him on your instructions?

They could see anything they wanted. As the hon. member for Kamloops knows, that was dramatically shown on the occasion when the hon. member for Winnipeg North felt that he had not seen everything he should have seen at No. 25 ordnance depot. He went back. He is a chartered accountant, he saw everything he wanted to see and came back and reported to the committee on defence expenditure that he did not know of any way in which the system could be improved.

The guards are on the right of the infantry but they do not change the infantry's place with relation to other formations. I will have something more to say about some of the points he raised.

I thought the hon. member for Prince Albert gave a magnificent and moving account of the progress made by NATO and I do express to him most sincere congratulations upon having made such good use of his time and having given us such a useful report. However, he did talk about strategic roads which seemed to me to have a slightly remote association with NATO. He also suggested that at some stage I had indicated that we would never be attacked by air, that I had ridiculed the idea of air attack against us. I have said a great deal in the house and outside about defence but I doubt if I ever made such a statement. In fact I can point to statements from 1946 onwards in the directly contrary sense, statements indicating that we had to build up our defences against air attack, and ever since 1946 the objectives of our defence have been about the same as they are today. Then he also charged me with not agreeing with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich when he suggested that we should spend $3 on the air force for every dollar on the army. That was said on the 18th of November, 1949.
I have looked up the discussion and I remember it very well. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, or the hon. member for Nanaimo as he was better known to us, did say that, but I did not make the reply that the hon. member for Prince Albert said I made. What I said was, and my reply can be seen in the discussion at that time, was that at that time we could not do it because we were spending only $195 million on defence. Therefore if we had done what the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich wanted us to do we would have had to wipe out the navy and the army, and I was not prepared to do so that day.
But since then events have changed, and I hope a lot of us have changed our thinking because the change has been a very dramatic and considerable one. Since then the extent of our defence expenditures has increased tenfold, I regret to say, from under $200 million in 1948-49 to something of the magnitude of $2 billion in 1953-54 or 1954-55. A

Supply-National Defence very great part of the increase since the beginning of the build-up in 1950 after Korea has been due to our increased effort in the air. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich can accept my full congratulations on having the right idea but not the right kind of money with which to afford it at the time. Since then developments have occurred as I have mentioned.
The hon. member for Prince Albert also said that he did not see how opposition members could appreciate the defence effort unless they were shown the actual production. Well, I say to hon. members: Go to No. 25 Canadian ordnance depot and see the tanks lined up in rows. Go to St. Hubert airport and see the Sabre fighters bound for overseas, more than a thousand delivered, on the way to the places where they are needed. Go to Avro and see the CF-100's and then move around the country, as I hope you all will, and see the radar stations with the latest in electronic equipment. Go and see it. I invite you, as I have repeatedly done in the past. There is nothing to prevent any member of parliament from going anywhere to see our defences. I encourage it. If you will only let the commanding officer of the district, air command or myself know, we will facilitate the arrangements either for groups or for individual members at any time. Let us make sure that you really do see what is going on.

He expressed some concern about our spending $34 a pair for skates for the teams. Apparently he is in the same position as I am-he has not bought skates for his children for a long time. These skates were purchased through the Department of Defence Production for the use of the team, in the same way as every other college- Saint Jean's is a college-does. It seems, however, that we did not pay quite as much for them as some colleges do. I made inquiries during the dinner hour, and I found that an Ottawa school paid $40 to $45 a pair for skates. These are about the quality of skates that are used by junior teams. It is the practice now for our colleges to be provided with some funds with which to buy sporting equipment in the same way as other colleges and schools have that equipment supplied. Some of these funds for that purpose apparently were used for these skates, but they got a little cheaper type than a local school does here.
Then he referred to the case of Kurt Meyer, and suggested that all Canadians convicted by courts-martial during the war, and still undergoing sentence, should be released.


There are no Canadians still serving sentences arising out of offences committed during the war. He then referred to the case of Private Cierpisz, which was referred to in the Globe and Mail. He should accept such statements, made in the course of the defence of that young man who was tried for his life, at something less perhaps than their full face value. This young man applied to join the armed forces. He gave a misstatement as to his age. He passed the aptitude test; he was taken in and he served. Then, he committed this offence for which he was sentenced to ten years. If any further details are required, I shall be glad to give them to the hon. gentleman outside the committee. I do not think it would be doing the case any particular good to go into it in great detail here.
Then, the hon. member for Calgary North said that I had been saying that our defences were grand, that our defences were adequate, everything was rosy, and that this had been my stock tactic throughout the years. I always asked the hon. member for Calgary North-I hope he will excuse it because we are very good friends-when I said those things; when I said them, where I said them, and what are the quotations,-
And I always indicated them.
-and he has never indicated them yet.
I always indicated them; I indicated them this afternoon.

He said we had no antiaircraft defence. Here, I am inclined to agree with him up to a certain point. At the present time, as I have indicated before, we are in a stage of transition. We have in Canada the latest anti-aircraft guns that there are. They are very expensive and the equipment, the predictor, the director, the tracking equipment and the firing equipment are very expensive. When you confront these guns with low flying high-speed jets or very high altitude jets, then their efficiency is much less than 100 per cent, let us say. We have been deliberately, as a deliberate calculated risk, not buying more of these guns and more of this equipment, but have that quantity which we think essential pending the arrival of ground-to-air rockets or guided missiles.
In that connection, of course, we have been following the United States and British work in this field. We have people working with them, and we have teams actually training with them. But there is not that type of equipment available yet in quantity for delivery.
With regard to airborne troops and aircraft, we have the aircraft necessary to carry

out the kind of lifts we consider is necessary to meet the kind of attack that might be made. This mobile striking force of three airborne divisions, artillery, engineers, medicals and the like, is not a brigade. It was originally planned as a brigade, but the concept changed and now it is planned to operate its units as three separate battalions. They are trained, and the exercises have shown that they do the job. In this connection, and in connection with civil defence to which other hon. members referred, I wish they could see and compare what we have in Canada with what there is in the various countries on the other side of the Atlantic, where the threat of an immediate attack and the consequences of an attack are far more imminent than they would be in our country.
I wish hon. members could compare our position with regard to defence against air attack, either by radar backed by fighters and anti-aircraft guns, civil defence and ground observers and so on, with the state of organization that there is on the other side of the ocean. They would be surprised at the considerable progress made on this side relative to the other.
Then the hon. member referred to the build-up of staffs, and so on. We set out in the white paper the distribution of the Canadian armed forces. I doubt if you could get this information for any other country, as between the various components engaged in defence operations. They are to be found there, divided among the effective fighting forces, the administrative and training staffs; those in Korea, Germany and the like. It is extremely difficult to generalize about these things. We strive continuously to cut down the overhead, the staffs, and to make continuous comparisons with the corresponding picture in the United States and Britain. So far as I know the results are generally favourable, despite the fact that we have relatively smaller forces. Still, this is a thing that I agree must be fought for steadily, to reduce the overhead, to reduce the cost and reduce manpower.
In this connection, we are faced with the perplexing problem of having adequate staffs to answer the questions on the order paper.

But what I do suggest is that at that time, in 1950, with the outbreak of the Korean war, and with Czechoslovakia just having been brought behind the iron curtain, there was, generally speaking, throughout this country, as in every other country, a feeling that war was likely to come upon us at any time. And we had to prepare *for that kind of emergency, as well as "the ilong pull". And Canada in this respect was somewhat unique. In the United States they have a system of government under which the administration can put forward estimates and requests for money which ultimately have to be dealt with by congress and which very frequently are changed in congress. These squadrons form an important element in the total defence there, and to withdraw them would mean leaving
