There is another reason, and that is that these Sabre fighters are really not well suited for the air defence of Canada. They have a relatively short range, they have only one pilot; they have not a complete set of navigational instruments, and if they went into the air and got into a dogfight in Canada they might have great difficulty in getting back to their airfield. If we had our fighter defence in Canada staffed by Sabre fighters it would mean that we would have to have our airfields for fighter defence at least twice and probably three times as numerous as they are today because of the very much shorter range of the aircraft. Along with double or triple the number of airfields at present in existence we would have to have an increase in their attendant facilities, such as runways, oil tanks, hangars, married quarters, and everything else. An airfield costs about $30 million, and we would also have to double or triple the number of emergency landing fields. In addition to that we would be faced with the necessity of maintaining Sabres and Sabre crews and training them for use in Canada as well as on the other side.
Therefore, from the point of view of our own defences this would not meet the need. The CF-100 does meet the need, and by the end of this year we will have all our regular squadrons, airfields, and radar stations operating on continental defence, which is the thing we have planned, and we will do it by about the time planned. That is the best and most economic way of carrying out this operation.

From this side of the house men have spoken who have had experience. There are men on the other side of the house who have had experience. It is a pity we do not have more speeches from the other side but that is the rub of the green. I have no doubt there are just as many on the other side of the house, but I say most earnestly that it is a great pity that such men have no chance to do anything except, after the policy is determined, to either approve or to criticize.
We are deprived of the judgment of these men. I think that is a great loss to the welfare of the state. I do not want to press the question of information but I want to say this. You can be fairly submerged with information of all kinds. You can go and look at things. It is no good for me to go and look at an aeroplane. All I know is how to get into an aeroplane and ride in it. My opinion on technical questions is of no value whatever.
We have people whose opinion would be of value. As I say, it is not a matter of the quantity of the information. The minister says, and I have no doubt correctly, that he has dished out information in great quantities. What I am suggesting is that we fail in this house, we entirely fail, to avail ourselves of the judgment of some of the best-informed and experienced people in this house on both sides. That is a great loss if we are losing that because of some blind worship of some technical shibboleth. I think it is a great pity.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I said I was going to be brief, and I shall be brief. I take

it at the moment, in spite of the billions we are spending, we cannot pretend to ourselves that we have any sense of urgency or widespread sense of public responsibility that we should have in order to meet this situation, and I think while that condition exists the government had better not take credit to itself and plume itself on the situation which exists.

I should like to bring just a few matters to the attention of the minister and the committee at this stage of the discussion. Before coming to the particular subject I want to mention that perhaps a comment or two on the minister's recent remarks might be in order. I was interested in the matter referred to lastly by the hon. member for Greenwood in that the minister said that he had given this parliament more information than any similar legislative body. This was in reference to a committee which might get at the root of the problem so as to enable parliament to deal in a more intelligent way with the problems of defence in Canada. I wonder if the minister really expects us to swallow that generalization?
Yes, I do.

Well, I do not intend to swallow it because some of us have made a study of what happens in other legislative bodies. I do not agree with the minister, to put it at its mildest, that this house gets more information than the United States congress does when it calls the secretary of defence before a committee, and not only the secretary of defence but the officers and the chiefs of staff. These people are subjected to questioning and the committee does not let them go until they answer the questions satisfactorily, questions of policy as well as masses of statistical information. The minister, I must admit, is prepared, and his department is prepared, to flood any committee we set up with a mass of statistical information. They bring it in in reams, and they are prepared to justify it. They justify their contracts. It does not matter if they have spent twice or three times the original estimate, they say that was inevitable and was all right because they got value for the money.
They are prepared to bring in all kinds of that information and to set up their experts to justify it. However we are not allowed to get at the type of witness the United States congress or British parliament brings before committees and compels to answer questions, the sort of questions on defence matters upon which we want information.
I take issue, too, with the minister's refusal to make available to this house the report of the three distinguished officers who have recently been making a survey of the situation with respect to the reserve army. The
Supply-National Defence minister said that would be, to paraphrase his words, a denial of the whole system of responsible government. We have heard some half-baked arguments on that subject before from such experts as the Secretary of State, whose job it was to keep information from parliament before he became a member. The justification in the past for that sort of refusal of that type of information which did not properly come to parliament was that it was confidential reports of civil servants to their ministers. There may be an argument -I am not admitting that I go along all the way with everything that is said in defence of the government there-but there may be room for argument or room for enormous difference of opinion.
However that is a very different thing from the minister spending public money, over and above what is called for by the estimate, or for civil servants who are on the staff of the department and who are of course the confidential advisers of the minister and upon whose advice he relies-it is a different thing from saying that we are not satisfied with the situation in the reserve army and so take it upon ourselves to obtain outside advice. Then, having set up this special committee, to say that the information derived as the result of the expenditure of public money shall be denied to parliament is, itself, a denial of responsible government. Yet, that is the sort of generality and absurdity with which the minister expects this committee to be satisfied in connection with the study of his estimates.
There can be only one reason why this report is refused, and that is that the government knows that it reveals a situation in connection with the reserve forces that is not satisfactory. Why does the government not admit it, and just tell us where it is not satisfactory and what efforts they intend to make to deal with the situation. Then, we would know not only where the cause for dissatisfaction lies, but what remedies were being proposed and instituted to deal with it. How much longer does the minister expect us to go on being satisfied with his general assurance that they are taking action to deal with this situation, when the situation in fact in the reserve forces is such as we have had revealed tonight by those with knowledge of the situation. The minister expects us to swallow too much if he expects us to swallow that whale.
There were one or two other perhaps minor points in the statement the minister has just delivered with which I suggest he has affronted this committee, and they are typical of the arguments which he uses all the way through. I feel that a reference to

Supply-National Defence them may illustrate the weakness of his whole position. He referred to the suggestion which had been made regarding bringing back some of the F-86 squadrons from Europe so that they might assist in the process of continental defence. Now, I do not go along completely with the suggestion that these squadrons should be brought back, although I do go along with the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich in his criticism in which he questioned the wisdom of denuding the defence of Canada, from the point of view of fighter aircraft, at the expense of building up strength overseas. The reasons given by the minister as to why it would not be appropriate to bring back these squadrons are so absurd that, as I say, they serve as an illustration of the whole statement with which he affronted us a few moments ago. He said they are not satisfactory for Canadian defence. They have only one pilot and if they get into a dogfight, with the prevalence of cloud and so on, it would be very difficult for them to find their way down again. I have never heard it suggested, Mr. Chairman, there is more cloud in Canada than there is in Europe.
There is more space.

More space, yes, there is more space. What does the United States rely upon for continental defence? Do they use the CF-100? Are they not as concerned as we are about the matter of continental defence? That is the sort of half-baked, half-reasoned argument with which the minister-
No part of the United States corresponds to every part of Canada, nor does the continental-
What did the minister say?
No part of the United States corresponds to the area across Canada, with our northern territory-

There is Alaska and the American bases in Newfoundland and Labrador. Why, good heavens, you would think the minister did not know that the United States has the far northern bases. They have a number of bases all over the world.

Their airfields are close
together there.
We have airfields in Canada.
Not nearly as many or as close.
I suppose the minister could go on-
I could elaborate on that, yes.
It comes back to the fact that the minister said they might get lost in the clouds.
He did not say that.
He most certainly did. I think the hon. gentleman was not in the house when he said it.

He was in the house
throughout the whole of the minister's speech and he listened carefully to the minister's speech.

That was what the minister said, and the hon. member is not going to change it by shouting. Because I say that was one of the main difficulties to which the minister referred.
Then the minister did not deal adequately -indeed, he hardly dealt with it at all- with the very thoughtful and excellent speech delivered last night by the hon. member for Queens. The hon. member made certain criticisms of the expensive policies followed by this government in connection with the building of jet engines. I think it should be emphasized that the suggestion of the hon. member for Queens was in no way that we should not build jet engines in Canada; in no way did he suggest that it was not desirable for us to have an aircraft engine industry. His suggestion was rather that, as has been done in the United States-and that is a particularly notable example where they desired to obtain experience in the building of jet engines-we should build under licence, from designs of countries which had already had experience in that work. Indeed experts in the field of aircraft engineering have told me that the main reason the Americans are now able to produce excellent jet engines in large quantities is because of the experience they were willing to acquire in the first instance, by building engines under licence.
And the point is that they acquired that experience at far less cost, and went into large-scale production in a great deal less time than would have been possible had they started from scratch, as we did here. And I do not think anything the minister has said thus far has even begun to deal with the points made last night by the hon. member for Queens, to the effect that engines are available to be built in Canada, under licence, capable of delivering a far greater thrust, and with far lower fuel consumption ratio, and waste ratio, than in respect of those being built in Canada at the present time.

May I just say this, that assuming what the hon. member says is correct-and it is not-it would take eighteen

months to two years from now to get into production of that type of engine; whereas we are probably producing as many jet engines as any country in the world today, except the United States.
But this by no means is the first time it has been suggested. This is not the first time the suggestion has been made. It was made more than eighteen months ago.
No.
Yes, indeed, it was, and not only publicly but privately. As the minister well knows, that criticism has been made privately; but it was not regarded because of some fetish they had-
Fetish?
-that they had in mind in the government and the department.
All we want is good engines.

Well, again that is the sort of generalization in which the minister indulges, but it does not deal with the statistics produced last night by the hon. member for Queens. Certainly the hon. member dealt with those statistics in an intelligent manner. The inference in the minister's last remark simply does not stand up, because the inference in that remark is that the engines described by the hon. member for Queens were not good ones. Well, the statistics he produced indicated that they are better than the ones being produced here. And I say those statistics should be dealt with before we are asked to accept the general assurances with which the minister expects us to be satisfied.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that there should be some further reference to the speech delivered on April 29 by Representative Sterling Cole to which reference was made last night by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich. This speech was delivered in New York at the 135th anniversary banquet of Colgate University. As has been pointed out, and should be emphasized, Representative Cole is chairman of the joint committee on atomic energy of the United States congress. The minister has given us the assurance that, notwithstanding what is contained in the remarks of Representative Cole, there are no negotiations between Canada and the United States which are now pending and, further than that, as I understand him, that there is no suggested construction in connection with the continental defence system and radar screen which is being held up by current negotiations, and by failure to pursue and to conclude those negotiations.
Supply-National Defence
Well that is in direct conflict with the statement contained in this speech. It is obvious from the terms of the speech and the occasion of its delivery that Representative Cole took this opportunity, on April 29, to lay before his country what he considered to be a grave and acute problem arising out of shortcomings in the continental defence effort of Canada and the United States. So these were not any passing or careless remarks.
I have the text of his speech here, and the whole of these seven single-spaced foolscap pages is devoted exclusively to this subject. I wish to make that clear, because I think it should be emphasized that this was a careful, considered and reasoned discussion of the subject of continental defence. And there are some very disturbing passages in this text. Reading now from the third to last paragraph on page 2 I find this:
The grim statistics are these: Today, the Soviet dictators are capable of manufacturing nuclear weapons of such destructive power that a single bomb could destroy the heart of New York or Chicago or Washington. Today, the Soviet union has planes capable of delivering such weapons- even if on one-way missions-against the majority of our critical target areas. Whether the Soviets could now mount an attack of such intensity and scope that our ability to retaliate would be eliminated may be open to debate. But three or four years from now, the Soviets will be able to launch a saturation attack against our nation-an attack so massive that our ability ultimately to prevail may be open to grave question.
Were an attack to occur this week, or this year, we would have no effective way of repelling it.
I would ask hon. members to contrast this paragraph with the statement made by the minister concerning a test he observed-a statement he has now modified to some extent, but which now stands on the record-concerning the ability of our defensive screen to deal with attacking enemy aircraft. I quote the minister as follows from page 4905 of Hansard:
It was not one hundred per cent but it was above 90 per cent indicating a very successful operational state.
And then, here is what Representative Cole said:
Were an attack to occur this week, or this year, we would have no effective way of repelling it. At best-and this is very optimistic-we might intercept as many as one out of every four Soviet bombers.
One out of every four, or 25 per cent success, is a very long way from 90 per cent success. And yet this speech is dealing with the very interception and defensive screen the Minister of National Defence was discussing yesterday.
No.

"No"? What one does this deal with, then?

Supply-National Defence
No; that is dealing with air defence of the United States, which not only includes the part of it that goes through Canada, but also both coasts.

Well, now, that is very interesting. I shall read on and see if hon. members take the same interpretation from this speech as the minister does. He says:
At best-and this is very optimistic-we might intercept as many as one out of every four Soviet bombers. It is entirely possible, however, that the ratio of interception would be much less-and I assure you that in saying this I am not revealing any secrets to the Soviet union. The rulers of Russia are probably better aware of our present inability to defend ourselves adequately against an atomic attack than are the American people themselves.
Then going on to page 4:
If we are to defend ourselves against the planes of today and tomorrow, rather than the planes of yesterday, our first requirement is for advance warning of an impending attack. Today we would have no more than a few minutes prior notice of approaching bomber formations.
Well, I assume that the representative must know that they have this screen in Canada to which the minister referred. He goes on:
My own belief is that we imperatively need at least six hours of advance warning.
Then, a further paragraph:
Space, sheer space, can be-if it is wisely used, an ally of untold worth in creating an effective continental defence system. Almost four years have passed since our scientists first proposed putting space to work by establishing an early warning line across the north of Canada and extending it seaward to the east and the west by means of patrol aircraft and picket ships. More than two years have passed since the formidable technical problems involved in making a distant warning system both effective and economical were surmounted. And yet, four years after the need for such an early warning line was pointed out, and two years after our scientists developed the equipment which would make such a line possible, it is still not in existence.
Now, sir, relating that fact to the earlier paragraph where he says we might intercept as many as one out of every four Soviet bombers, I suggest it is absolutely impossible to conclude that the representative did not have in mind the defence screen line in Canada when he made that statement. He concludes the paragraph from which I was last quoting with the quotation already placed on record by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich:
Negotiations with the Canadian government on the subject of where, how and by whom the first of such early warning lines would be built and operated have been in progress for nearly two years.
Representative Cole went on to point out -and I am just going to summarize the rest of his remarks-that Canada and the United States have a joint stake in this matter of


continental defence. That of course has been recognized in principle by the remarks of the minister not only in this debate but in others, and that view is of course shared also by all hon. members. But the whole point of the speech made by Representative Cole is that as yet.-although he comes fairly close to suggesting that we are to blame; he does not say so specifically, I think for obvious reasons-we have not even really begun to build up an effective radar or early warning system on this continent. This committee and the country is entitled to know that, and the situation indeed simply demands a much more complete statement from the minister of the situation than that with which we have so far been furnished, because there is too big a contrast between the statement emphasized, the facts outlined and underlined by Representative Cole, and the possibility that we would be lucky if we could intercept one out of every four enemy bombers, and the statement of the minister last night and modified to some extent this afternoon that our early warning device would enable us to intercept approximately nine out of ten aircraft. In the absence of anything further than what we have heard so far, Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that this is another of the minister's vague general assurances.

speechtext: Is it the view of the committee that we shall now proceed to the estimates by subheadings?

During the remarks I made yesterday I called attention to the fact that the white paper of 1951 forecast that there would be some of the four escort vessels launched by the end of 1951 or at the latest the beginning of 1952, and that the white paper of this year gave the fact that five had actually been launched by March 31 of this year. I ask for some information as to what seems to be a very considerable delay and a very considerable difference in the forecast of 1951 and the results of performance as shown by the launching of the five vessels by March 31 of this year. I presume that the four which were intended to be launched in 1951 are included in the five which have actually been launched.
I wonder whether the minister could give the committee some idea as to the reasons for that forecast which proved so inaccurate in 1951, and the reasons for the very long delay there has been in producing more than five of the fourteen vessels. I must call attention to the fact that these vessels are not commissioned now; they have merely been launched, and there is a long period of many, many months usually between the

launching of a vessel and its commissioning. I would ask the minister whether he would give some idea-I hope a fairly accurate forecast-of when those five vessels which have now been launched may be commissioned and when the remaining nine which he has given a forecast of being launched by the end of this year may expect to be commissioned so that we may see when the fourteen escort vessels which were included in this three-year plan may really be ready to take their places with the Royal Canadian Navy in its duties either of escort, or of employment with Canada's forces with NATO.

I have that information
though not in quite as full detail as the hon. member has asked for it. I wonder whether we can take it up when we come to the navy headings, but in a general way I can tell him that the main reason, as I have been informed, for the delay in the construction of those vessels was, as I said the other night, that they are a completely new type, new design, and have a power plant which is quite unique. We wanted to produce the power plant in Canada, but in order to get on with the job we bought the first one in Britain. There was delay in securing delivery, and in installing it there was further delay. Now we are well advanced, and I think the delivery dates for all fourteen will be compressed, so that instead of spreading them out as would have been the case fairly evenly at the beginning we shall begin commissioning the first next year, and the others will follow quite rapidly afterwards. The anticipation is that we shall commission those ships probably about five or six years after laying down the keels; whereas, as indicated in the case of corresponding ships in Britain and in the United States, they have had similar delays and will take a bit longer.
One of the reasons for this is that the type of vessel, the electronic equipment, the guns, the antisubmarine equipment, the wiring and the power plants have all been under process of design throughout the period of construction in order to get on with the job, and this proved to be a very complicated operation.

Have you plans so that you will have the crews available next year when these ships are commissioned? According to the last figures of the naval enlistment strength of the Royal Canadian Navy, we are rather short of the target which has been set, and I presume that would include these crews.

We will have the crews. The most difficult element in the crews are the engine room staff, electronics, wireless and
Supply-National Defence so on, but these key men have been undergoing training in the United Kingdom as well as here.

Just one moment, Mr. Chairman. I regret to find it necessary to rise again before we pass on to the details. We had a detailed analysis of the defence situation by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saan-ich yesterday, and we had a detailed analysis in regard to the armoured units by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, and we have had a very exact statement in so far as anti-aircraft are concerned by the hon. member for Calgary North. But the minister has completely skirted around these statements.
In answer to a statement that with all this expenditure we have practically no anti-aircraft, except possibly two batteries, one on the east coast and one on the west coast, equipped with, so far as one knows, weapons far from the description given by the minister, we are told about our having the best antiaircraft guns in the world. But where are they? Where are the units? That is what we want to know. We have spent $5,500 million, not since the end of the war but during this period. Now, where is the defence in Canada representing that money. Where are these anti-aircraft batteries at a time when they are an essential part of our defence? What are the use of radar screens unless they bring into action not only the aircraft but the anti-aircraft gun at the appropriate point? I am not going to go into further details in regard to these anti-aircraft guns lest it be suggested that asking more questions might involve some secrecy. But I am going to say they are not in a position to feed those guns at the moment.
In so far as the units of the reserve forces are concerned, instead of dealing with a specific statement that these units are not up to their authorized strength, the minister sought to convey the impression that the only thing that was wrong was that they were not up to their full strength. No one at any time in this debate suggested that we expect the units to be up to full strength. There is a strength laid down by the Department of National Defence. Either they come within striking distance of that figure or there should be a general readjustment of the general training plan. Either that is the figure that is going to be employed or the training plan defeats itself. If you only have a quarter of those who are expected to carry out a certain training program then that training program becomes nearly wholly ineffective in so far as the original purpose is concerned.

Supply-National Defence
To give an illustration and only an illustration, .seven artillery regiments will be kept as one group at Petawawa this year. I pointed out this was no mere case of not being up to the authorized strength. I pointed out that of these seven regiments only one of these trained two batteries instead of three, which would make a regiment, and that so far as the other batteries are concerned some would train one battery instead of three, and some only a single troop and that represents one of the better artillery groups in the country. What is the answer to that?
It is not enough to say we are not up to full strength. The very inequality of these units makes that training extremely difficult to carry out. How can regimental headquarters be trained if they never have one troop of a battery in training? The whole thing is so disproportionate in cost, in training, and in the result of that training. I pointed out that so far as the batteries actually in camp are concerned that these batteries would have a complement of possibly 120 guns and they fire 24.
Either we really mean business about the training of the reserves or we do not. If we do not then let us admit it. If we do then let us establish a training plan that can actually be carried into effect. That is all that is suggested. The officers are keen, the N.C.O.'s are keen and the men are anxious to do their job. But the plan obviously is not working, and it is in relation to that plan that there is a report from three competent officers. The answer given by the minister that this is a confidential report to the staff is really not describable in terms that would be permitted under the rules of this house.
That is a report that really challenges the responsibility of the members of this house. It is in relation, I believe, to this very breakdown in the pattern of our reserve training that these officers were appointed. How can we pass on any details, how can we say that a certain estimate of money for the training of reserve units should or should not be allowed when we cannot see the reports of the officers appointed to examine into this and to make their recommendations?
The idea that this is something confidential which should not be shown to the public is such nonsense that no such statement should have been made in this house. I cannot help going back to the time when there was not this pretence about the secrecy of recommendations. There was a very interesting report by Sir William Otter dated January 27,


1912. As those who have followed the training for some years will remember, General Otter was largely responsible for the reorganization of the reserve forces before the first world war. It was largely because of the fact that his recommendations were followed, his recommendation on a sixth divisional organization of balanced complement of infantry, cavalry, engineers and artillery, that it was possible for Canada to send the first division, not a division alone, but over 30,000 men, overseas no less than two months after the sudden and unexpected outbreak of that war. I would like to read the closing paragraph of that particular report by Sir William Otter. I might add that I am quoting from sessional paper number 35 of this house for the year 1913. The closing paragraph of that report is paragraph 197, and it reads as follows-but might I ask hon. members to listen to how up-to-date the wording sounds:
Have not the plaudits awarded for a church or ceremonial parade lulled us into the belief that we are fit and capable for any military strain coincident with invasion, and in the continuance of that assumption, are we not encouraging a rude awakening some day, to find ourselves far short of such a consummation, with the result, irreparable loss?
Mr. Chairman, that was a warning at that time. The warning on that occasion was acted upon, fortunately for the capacity of this country to meet the test at a time when that contribution was extremely important.
The repetition by the minister of statements already made by every hon. member who has spoken, to the effect that our men on active service, in the permanent force, have a type of training which gives us reason for pride as does the manner in which they are conducting themselves, must not be allowed to divert the attention of any hon. members from the fact that the central feature of this discussion has been the reserve training which is recognized as the backbone of our defence and without which the forces now overseas or the forces in the permanent army, air force or navy could not hope to carry out their responsibilities.
Certainly it stirs us to speak with pride of these young Canadians. Those on this side of the chamber speak about it with just as much feeling, confidence and admiration as does anyone on the other side of this chamber. After all, there are members of the family of those on this side of the chamber as well as those on the other side who share that experience. There are a number of us who have had the privilege of visiting these establishments away from Canada and of seeing what is being done there. The very

fact that we can produce units like that is all the more reason why we should decide to get down to brass tacks with regard to the reserve army.
Not one word the minister has said tonight has offered an answer or has given any explanation of the failure of the plans of this government, except one; and if that is the answer, then it is time the minister made another speech to outline completely new plans. What he said was-this is the only point on which he came close to reality with regard to the reserve army-that there is a different situation today from that which was in existence at the time the reserve or militia units, as they were then called, were really up to authorized strength. There is a different situation today. Let us make no mistake about that.
Pie said that the difference now is that we have a large regular force instead of the few thousand that there were at that time. That is true. We might also recall that this is a much more populous country today. We also might recall that the number of men in the actual service units is only a fraction of the figure that is constantly put before us of the total in the regular force. Let us grasp that fact. The number of young men in the permanent force who are actually in service units is only a fraction of the total that is put before us as the evidence of our contribution in this field. In fact, on the basis of any explanation given, it is still impossible to understand why we need such an enormous staff and training organization for the number we actually have. We are still waiting for some explanation of that situation.
I must say that there is one place where we do not fail, namely, in the spending of money. For instance, we have just learned that Canada is going to spend large sums on a military building in Washington. I do not know whether there is any arrangement by which we are going to have an army of occupation there. Certainly it is difficult to understand why we need to spend more than $2 million for a building down there unless we are contemplating a substantial movement to the United States of armed forces to be served by those who would be going there. Even at present rates you can build something fairly substantial for $2 million; and it is not likely that that figure will be the real one.
Mr. Chairman, not one explanation that has been given has gone to the core of this problem, namely that whatever plans are made should be realistic ones and that there is no reason why this country cannot maintain the reserve forces at the full strength now authorized. May I repeat that I am not
Supply-National Defence saying it should be "at full service strength"; I am saying "at the full strength authorized by the Department of National Defence" and presumably at a figure that they believe will be in camp or will be trained locally. In fact, there could be no justification for carrying out this training on this basis unless that is the intention of the government.
Let us have some explanation of why we carry on with these ineffective plans. Let us find out why it is that there are these discrepancies. Let us know not that there are a number of tanks that can be seen lined up in the way the minister has described tonight. Let us have an answer to the explanation given by an experienced tank officer that there is wholly inadequate armoured training in this country at the present time. It is not tanks in mothballs that we want. It is armoured units trained to use the tanks. That is what we are not getting at this time.
Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that this committee should proceed to the detailed estimates until we have from the minister an answer that does not skirt around this vitally important problem of the training of the reserve and recruitment for the reserve. In spite of what has already been said, I also think we should have before us the report of the three officers who have considered this subject. In this matter I think hon. members opposite have the heaviest responsibility, because they are the ones who can demand it. I would urge them to consider the responsibility of every hon. member in this committee in passing on detailed estimates with regard to reserve training and other training when we do not get the report which every one of us knows deals with this very problem and which in itself may give the answer to this question.
I would hope that the minister wou'd consider this matter over the week end-it is now eleven o'clock-and that when we meet on Monday he will have reconsidered the question of this report which justifies no such secrecy as that with which he is surrounding it. Moreover, I would hope that he will take us sufficiently into his confidence to justify the belief on the part of hon. members that they have at least the basic information required to approach these detailed items with some knowledge of the facts.

Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition has repeated once more what he said earlier and what was said by other hon. members. I repeat what I said, namely that it was my hope that we would have the consideration of this report sufficiently advanced that we could study the reserve

Business of the House
army when we reach the details which appear at page 308 of the estimates. That is what I said and that is what appears in Hansard. I repeat it.
Does the minister now mean that we are going to get the whole report?
No. Of course not.
We are going to get the report according to the revised version of the Minister of National Defence.
What you are going to get is the decision of the department of the government.
Which tells us nothing.

No, no. It just tells you what we have decided. We take the responsibility of acting on the advice. We take the responsibility of asking for the advice and I take the responsibility of not giving the source of information that is given to me, not on a confidential basis but what is actually marked "secret".
Hear, hear.
Every hon. member who is now applauding this evasion-
Hear, hear.
Every hon. member who is now applauding this evasion is going to be asked-
Hear, hear.

-to pass on these statements without any of the basic information, and we do not know whether or not that report is marked "secret".
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have made good progress this week and I think we can make better progress next week. There is on Votes and Proceedings notice of a resolution
having to do with the Public Service Superannuation Act. It will be called for His Excellency's signification of his consent on Monday and we would like to proceed with it on either Tuesday or Wednesday so as to have second reading and refer it to the banking and commerce committee for consideration on Thursday, if possible. Subject to that, the business on Monday and Tuesday will be as follows: Second reading of an act respecting inventions by public servants; the resolution with respect to crown corporations; second reading of an act to amend the Radio Act; second reading of an act to amend the National Harbours Board Act; second reading of an act to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act; the resolution with respect to disability pensions; continuation of the debate on second reading of an act to amend the Research Council Act.
When we conclude those items we shall take the budget resolutions, and if all this is concluded before Tuesday night we shall move to go into supply. On Wednesday it will be the intention to take the bills reported from the banking and commerce committee, namely, the Bank of Canada Act, an act respecting banks and banking and the Quebec Savings Banks Act. On Thursday and Friday we shall take interim supply to begin with and then the departments of transport, justice, secretary of state and agriculture.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: While we are on the business of the house, may I say a word or two. I hope that the leader of the house will not take it from the fact that we did not draw attention to the fact that it was ten o'clock sixty-five minutes ago that we will adopt the same attitude all next week. Some of us feel that if it is the desire to extend the length of the sitting day it should be done by a proper motion, and speaking for those of us in this group we would rather see that extension in the morning than at night.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I move that the house do now adjourn.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 11.05 p.m.

Monday, May 24, 1954
